# 4.3: Production-Inventory Planning: Single Product

ISE 754: Logistics Engineering, Fall 2026

The interdependence of production decisions quickly overwhelms simple planning rules. For these complex problems, reliable heuristics are rarely available. MILP provides the essential framework to systematically evaluate every trade-off and identify the optimal plan.

No new Julia packages used.

No new Logjam functions used.

Companion script

4-net-3.jl, runnable Julia extracted from the lecture’s code blocks.

## 1. Production-inventory planning

Production-inventory planning models are a primary application of mathematical programming in industry. They provide a means to make complex decisions over a rolling planning horizon. Decisions are complex because each has an impact across multiple time periods and stages in the production process. Reliable heuristics are rarely available. A time-expanded network is used to model multi-period production-inventory problems. Models are re-solved each time period, using the latest mix of firm and forecasted orders over the planning horizon.

Among the Networks models, production-inventory planning stands somewhat apart, because it leaves the geographic representation of a problem behind. A production-inventory problem has two dimensions: time, since production is planned over several periods, and the stages of production, the output of each stage feeding the next until the last sends the product to the customer. The stages need not all occur in the same period, and when they do not, the product is carried as inventory at a real cost, to be weighed against the cost of production. What makes the problem interesting is that the resources are capacitated, which makes it a tactical problem rather than a strategic one: how much capacity to build is not being determined, and the problem is how best to deploy the capacity available to produce a series of products. Once setup costs (Sec. 3) or several products (Lecture 4.4) are part of it, it is the one point in the course where a mixed-integer linear program is really needed, since there are no good heuristics for the problem and no other way of looking at it. The uncapacitated facility location (UFL) problem was also solved as a mixed-integer linear program (Lecture 2.7), but there it was more than was needed, since a good heuristic exists for it (Lecture 2.4), and a mixed-integer linear program is worth using for the UFL only when constraints are added that a heuristic would find hard to incorporate.

Production-inventory planning is the core of the course: if the course covered nothing else, this would be the one thing to cover.

NoteHow planning software grows

Much of it is embedded in the software used in logistics engineering, so only a developer at one of the companies that build the software works with the models directly. A field engineer, dealing with a client’s problems, still has to know enough of it to judge whether a problem, a constraint, or some other aspect of the client’s supply chain or logistics network can be modeled. Sometimes the model already has the capability and it is easily done. The interesting cases are those where it does not, and the client is large enough that the capability is developed for it. That is how such software evolves: nobody designs it from scratch; it grows one project after another, each slightly different from the last, and a solution to one client’s particular problem is easy to generalize for the next. After ten to twenty years of this, a commercial product has its full feature set.

A single product, with a model that handles that product alone, is the place to start; Lecture 4.4 treats multiple products that share some of the resources, where how they share them is determined within the model.

Decisions in these models are complex because each one affects several periods and stages. A production-inventory model is needed only when a decision made now limits what can be done later: with weekly periods, a decision made this week can rule out something three weeks from now. A system in which everything happens within a couple of hours, and in which any decision can be redone, never needs one. The models suit production that is committed once it is set up, such as a refinery set up for one kind of product, and resources with long scheduled downtime: a two-month maintenance shutdown is planned years ahead, and since the low-demand season is too short to maintain every resource in it, when each one is maintained is itself a decision. Decisions like these soon outrun any feel for a good answer, which leaves a planner more reliant on the models than in most problems. Road networks and location problems can be seen on a map; production-inventory problems cannot be visualized well, and the mathematical program is the best way of looking at them.

Demand is handled differently here than in the rest of the course. The earlier lectures assumed a constant demand, as strategic problems typically do, since they seldom need to incorporate variability at all, and two of the Inventory lectures (Lectures 6.1 and 6.2) model variability explicitly. Production-inventory planning is a middle ground: its models are deterministic, but they handle variability by having a different demand in each period over the planning horizon. That handles both the variability and the need for a deterministic model, without stochastic programming or simulation, neither of which can handle models as complex as production-inventory models can be.

Lecture 1.3 also assumed a constant average demand, and captured variability through the factory-physics equations, among them the VUT (variability, utilization, time) equation for cycle time (Eq. 6 in Lecture 1.3). That is a different type of variability from the one considered here. The variability here is structural: it is deterministic in each period, and the different demand in each period captures it.

Although technically the capacity is variable, it is really not variable: it is either available or not available. In Sec. 2, the decision about whether capacity is available or not is made outside of the model. Prior to effective mixed-integer linear programming, this was the only way these kinds of problems could be solved. A logistics engineer would have to make the capacity decisions, and capacity that is not available would just be set to zero. Then this would be solved as a linear program, which was doable even in the 1980s. Making the decision internally to the model, the subject of Sec. 3 on setup costs, was only possible when mixed-integer linear programming capability came online in the early to mid 1990s. The setup costs were also there in the problems of Sec. 2, but the cost of the setups was not needed because the setups had already been made outside the model. This is an important distinction, and the whole point of this lecture.

Neither the planning horizon nor the demand over it is given to a logistics engineer. As with many things, determining an appropriate planning horizon is the engineer’s responsibility, and part of the whole process of engineering a solution to a production-inventory problem. There is not necessarily a single answer: different engineers can arrive at different horizons, some better than others. Forecasting the demand over the horizon is part of the same responsibility. The examples of Secs. 2 and 3 are given their horizon and their demand, so that the focus is on the models; Sec. 4 then takes up where the demand comes from, and Sec. 5 how long the horizon should be.

The time-expanded network of Fig. 1 is the basic setup of every production-inventory model, and understanding it is most of what is needed to understand the models. It is the network of a single product. Each row of nodes is a stage of production, two in the figure, and each column a period being planned, typically a week or a month; a year would usually be too long. The most important input is the demand forecast for each period. The current period’s demand, 20 tons in the figure, is probably all orders already received, so it is a very good number; the second period’s is perhaps two-thirds booked orders and one-third forecast, the third’s one-third booked and two-thirds forecast, and further out more and more of it is forecast, until all of it is. With monthly periods the model is re-solved every month with the actual orders and the best forecast of the rest, and each solution says how production is to run, above all in the current period: how much to produce at each stage, how much of it meets demand, and how much is carried into the next period as inventory. Everything is measured in tons. The $x$ variables are the tons produced, and the $y$ variables the tons of inventory, the tons at a stage carried from one period into the next, where they can go on to the next stage and ultimately meet demand, or be carried again.

```julia
# Code block 1: drawing the time-expanded network of a production plan
# Stage i is row i and period j column j; each arc runs from node outline
# to node outline, and each label is a symbol in black with its value in
# red, as on the slide the figure is redrawn from; given a plan's
# production X and inventory Y, their values replace the capacities and
# the inventory symbols, in blue
ink, datac = colorant"#252525", colorant"#d21f26"
flowc = colorant"#1f5fa8"                         # a plan's flows
# Every symbol in the font of the lecture's equations, New Computer
# Modern: italic for the letter, upright for its digits and operators
mi = Makie.MathTeXEngine.texfont(:italic)
mr = Makie.MathTeXEngine.texfont(:math)
it(s) = rich(s; font = mi)                        # a symbol, in italics
up(s; kw...) = rich(s; font = mr, kw...)          # digits, operators
mth(s) = rich([isletter(c) ? it(string(c)) : up(string(c))
               for c in s]...)                    # a mixed term
sym(b, sub, sup = nothing) = sup === nothing ?    # b with subscript sub
    rich(it(b), subscript(up(sub))) :             #   and superscript sup
    rich(it(b), subsup(up(sub), mth(sup)))
num(v) = (r = round(v, digits = 2); isinteger(r) ? Int(r) : r)
val(v; c = datac) = up(" = $(num(v))"; color = c)      # a value
function drawpinet(cᵖ, u, cⁱ, d, y⁰, yᵗ⁺¹; X = nothing, Y = nothing,
                   unit = "month", w = 680, h = 500, r = 0.17, ls = 16,
                   dx = 2.3, dy = 2.0, g = 0.07)    # g: label to its arc
    m, t = length(cᵖ), length(d)
    fig = Figure(size = (w, h))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; aspect = DataAspect())
    hidedecorations!(ax); hidespines!(ax)
    P(i, j) = ((j - 1) * dx, -(i - 1) * dy)       # stage i, period j
    arc(p, q) = arrows2d!(ax, [p[1]], [p[2]], [q[1] - p[1]],
                          [q[2] - p[2]]; color = ink, shaftwidth = 1.3,
                          tipwidth = 8, tiplength = 8)
    lbl(p, s; al = (:left, :center), rot = 0.0, off = (0, 0)) =
        text!(ax, p[1], p[2]; text = s, color = ink, fontsize = ls,
              align = al, rotation = rot, offset = off)
    ℓ, ℓs = 1.0, 1.5                              # end arcs, supply arcs
    for j in 1:t
        x0, y0 = P(1, j)                          # supply into stage 1
        arc((x0, y0 + ℓs), (x0, y0 + r))
        for i in 1:m                              # production, stage i
            xa, ya = i == 1 ? (x0, y0 + ℓs) : P(i - 1, j) .- (0, r)
            ym = (ya + P(i, j)[2] + r) / 2
            lbl((xa + 0.1, ym + 0.2),
                rich(sym("c", "$i", "p"), val(cᵖ[i])))
            lbl((xa + 0.1, ym - 0.2), X === nothing ?
                rich(sym("x", "$i,$j"), up(" ≤ "), sym("u", "$i,$j"),
                     val(u[i, j])) :
                rich(sym("x", "$i,$j"), val(X[i, j]; c = flowc)))
            i > 1 && arc((xa, ya), P(i, j) .+ (0, r))
        end
        xm, ym = P(m, j)                          # demand out of stage m
        arc((xm, ym - r), (xm, ym - ℓ))
        lbl((xm, ym - ℓ - 0.22), rich(sym("d", "$j"), val(d[j]));
            al = (:center, :center))
    end
    for i in 1:m                                  # inventory arcs
        xa, ya = P(i, 1) .- (ℓ + 0.4, 0)          # initial
        xb = P(i, 1)[1] - r
        arc((xa, ya), (xb, ya))
        lbl(((xa + xb) / 2, ya + g),
            rich(sym("y", "$i,1"), up(" = "), sym("y", "$i", "0"));
            al = (:center, :bottom))
        lbl(((xa + xb) / 2, ya - g), val(y⁰[i]); al = (:center, :top))
        for j in 1:t-1
            p, q = P(i, j) .+ (r, 0), P(i, j + 1) .- (r, 0)
            arc(p, q)
            lbl(((p[1] + q[1]) / 2, p[2] + g),        # cost, just above
                rich(sym("c", "$i", "i"), val(cⁱ[i]));
                al = (:center, :bottom))
            # flow, below; a y alone has no tall glyph, so it is raised by
            # about half its font size, which puts its top as close to its
            # arc as the tops of the values below the other arcs
            lbl(((p[1] + q[1]) / 2, p[2] - g), Y === nothing ?
                sym("y", "$i,$(j+1)") :
                rich(sym("y", "$i,$(j+1)"), val(Y[i, j+1]; c = flowc));
                al = (:center, :top),
                off = Y === nothing ? (0, 0.52ls) : (0, 0))
        end
        p = P(i, t) .+ (r, 0)                     # final
        q = p .+ (ℓ + 0.4 - r, 0)
        arc(p, q)
        lbl(((p[1] + q[1]) / 2, p[2] + g),
            rich(sym("y", "$i,$(t+1)"), up(" = "), sym("y", "$i", "t+1"));
            al = (:center, :bottom))
        lbl(((p[1] + q[1]) / 2, p[2] - g), val(yᵗ⁺¹[i]);
            al = (:center, :top))
    end
    for i in 1:m, j in 1:t                        # nodes, over the arcs
        poly!(ax, Circle(Point2f(P(i, j)...), r); color = :white,
              strokecolor = ink, strokewidth = 1.8)
    end
    xc = (t - 1) * dx / 2                         # what the arcs are
    lbl((xc, ℓs + 0.15), "Supply"; al = (:center, :bottom))
    yb = -(m - 1) * dy - ℓ - 0.55
    lbl((xc, yb), "Demand"; al = (:center, :top))
    for j in 1:t
        lbl((P(1, j)[1], yb - 0.4), "$j"; al = (:center, :top))
    end
    lbl((xc, yb - 0.75), "Period ($(unit))"; al = (:center, :top))
    xl = -(ℓ + 0.4) - 0.25
    lbl((xl, -(m - 1) * dy / 2), "Initial inventory";
        al = (:center, :bottom), rot = π / 2)
    xr = (t - 1) * dx + ℓ + 0.4 + 0.25
    lbl((xr, -(m - 1) * dy / 2), "Final inventory"; al = (:center, :top),
        rot = π / 2)
    for i in 1:m
        lbl((xl - 0.55, P(i, 1)[2]), "$i"; al = (:center, :center))
    end
    lbl((xl - 0.85, -(m - 1) * dy / 2), "Stage"; al = (:center, :bottom),
        rot = π / 2)
    return fig
end

drawpinet([200, 800], [50 0 50; 60 0 0], [5, 25], [20, 10, 15], [0, 0],
          [35, 0])
```

Figure 1: The time-expanded network of a single product made in two stages over three monthly periods, with the data of Ex. 1. Production enters each stage’s node at a cost of $c_i^p$ per ton, up to the stage’s capacity $u_{ij}$ in the period; inventory $y_{ij}$ is carried from period $j-1$ to period $j$ at a cost of $c_i^i$ per ton; and the last stage meets each period’s demand $d_j$. Everything in black is a symbol, and everything in red its particular value. The horizontal arcs, left to right, are the inventory flows, and the vertical arcs, top to bottom, are the production flows.

## 2. Capacity determined outside the model

For a single product without setups, a plan can usually be found by hand, without a linear program: every arc of the time-expanded network points forward, so each ton can be made as late as capacity allows, working back from the last stage, by the procedure Model 2 states below. The procedure is exact only under its assumptions. A storage limit, an upper bound on the amount of inventory that can be carried from one period to the next, can break it: in Ex. 4 the latest plan would hold more at a stage than it can store, and only the linear program finds the plan that does not. Setup costs (Sec. 3) make which periods to produce in a decision of its own, which takes a mixed-integer linear program. The linear program, Model 1, is the model that carries these; the procedure is how a plan is found, and checked, by hand.

With several products (Lecture 4.4), the problem is formulated as an integer program, and there is no simple heuristic to rely on; that is where the solver is really needed.

For production-inventory problems in general, no heuristic is known short of solving the whole problem, because a decision made now affects what happens not only now but four, five, six, seven or eight periods later.

### 2.1 Linear program

The following production-inventory LP planning model is for a single product, produced in $m$ stages with a rolling horizon of $t$ periods (e.g., months). Determining if production capacity $u_{ij}$ should be available for each period, e.g., $u_{ij} = u_i$ or $u_{ij} = 0$ is used to plan production.

The first model is for a production system that produces a single product, and it makes no internal decision about what to produce when. What makes the problem more than trivial is that the resources are typically shared with other products, and the model stays a linear program by handling that through the capacities $u_{ij}$, the production capacity of stage $i$ in period $j$. In a period in which a resource is available for the product, all of its capacity is, say 10 tons a month; in other periods it makes other products. Which product to make is not determined by the model, since that is the multiple-product problem of Lecture 4.4; instead, the person operating the model sets the capacity to zero in each period in which the resource is not available. That is very labor-intensive, and with multiple products today’s solvers can simply solve the problem with that decision in it. Twenty or thirty years ago, before solver performance improved enormously, there was no other way than solving a lot of linear programs: the logistics engineer determined when to make capacity available, and the linear program then found, for those decisions, the best flow of product and how much of it to carry over as inventory, which still took a great many of the details off the engineer’s hands. Modeling the decision directly takes it away from the engineer altogether and makes still more complex problems possible. In the model, the objective is the unit production cost and the inventory carrying cost; the variables $x_{ij}$ are how much to produce at each stage in each period, continuous since the model is a linear program; and the variables $y_{ij}$ are the inventory carried from period to period. The superscript $p$ marks a production cost and $i$ an inventory cost. The network of Fig. 1 is the easiest way to understand the formulation.

Fig. 1 shows the model on its data, a network flow problem. Raw materials go into stage 1, and the first column of nodes is the first of three months. The arc into stage 1 in month 1 has an upper bound, its capacity $u_{1,1}$, here 50 tons, and a cost of \$200 per ton; $u_{1,2}$ is stage 1’s capacity in month 2, and so on. The initial inventory, $y_1^0$ at stage 1, is where the plan stands now, carried over from the previous run, since the linear program is re-solved every month: next month’s run makes month 2 the first month and extends the plan one month further, and the inventory on the horizontal arcs becomes the initial inventory of the new first month. Because the model is not run to infinity, the final inventory is the inventory wanted when the plan ends, and typically it is not zero: a final inventory of zero would not be realistic for an ongoing production process that is not being shut down in three months. An ongoing operation would also typically have a positive initial inventory; Fig. 1 sets it to zero for simplicity. At stage 2, production costs \$800 per ton, with a capacity of 60 tons, and the flow out of stage 2 is the demand, 20, 10 and 15 tons in the three months. Carrying a ton from month 1 to month 2 costs \$25 at stage 2, more than at stage 1, because \$800 more has been spent processing it. Some capacities are zero, stage 1’s in month 2 and stage 2’s in months 2 and 3, because the resource may be making another product then, or be down for scheduled maintenance.

What the stages mean in context is the steps of production, since production does not all happen at one point. Stage 1 might take the raw material, a metal or a plastic, and cast it into a particular form, and stage 2 take the casting and process it further, say trimming features off its edges that need correcting. A stage can also be the physical transportation of the product: the processing of one stage takes place at one location, and the product is then put on a plane and flown to another country for the next stage, perhaps a second operation, and then flown somewhere else again, so that a complex production process can easily have dozens of stages. The inventory cost reflects this. The product at stage 2 is in a sense the same product as at stage 1, but not really: \$200 has been spent to produce a ton of it at stage 1, and another \$800 at stage 2. Carrying a ton costs the carrying rate times what has been invested in it, so a ton at stage 2, carrying what was spent at both stages, costs more to carry than a ton at stage 1; Ex. 1 calculates the two costs, the \$5 and \$25 per ton of Fig. 1, in Eq. 2. In essence, each stage adds value. That is obvious in manufacturing, which changes the physical form of a product, but it applies as well to a product put in a shipping container in China when \$3,000 is spent to transport the container to the port of Long Beach: the \$3,000 is added to the value of all the products in the container.

So the product is worth more when it is taken off the ship in Los Angeles than when it left China. The difference is often small enough to ignore, but every manufacturing or transportation step adds value, even one that leaves the product physically unchanged, and that is how the inventory costs of Fig. 1 are to be read. The solver makes no use of the network’s structure; the model is solved simply as a linear program. For a single product, as here, it is a minimum cost network flow problem, Model 3 in Lecture 4.2. Once integer or binary variables are added (Sec. 3), it is no longer the classic minimum cost network flow problem, but as a linear program it is exactly that.

The question is how to do this at least cost. The two costs that can be minimized are the cost of production and the cost of inventory. At each node, the inventory carried in and what is produced are the input, and the output is either sent on to the next stage, used to satisfy demand, or carried over as inventory. Model 1 states the model in words and as a linear program.1

minimize: total production and inventory cost over the planning horizon

solve for:
(a) production at each stage in each period;
(b) inventory at each stage carried into each period.

subject to:
(a) flow balance at each stage that feeds the next: what is produced or carried in is either passed on to the next stage or carried out;
(b) flow balance at the last stage, which feeds demand: what is produced or carried in either meets the period’s demand or is carried out;
(c) capacity: production at each stage in each period is no more than its capacity;
(d) initial and final inventory: inventory at each stage at the start and at the end of the horizon is given;
(e) storage: inventory at each stage between periods is no more than its storage capacity.

assumptions:
(a) production cost and inventory cost per ton at each stage are constant;
(b) demand in each period is given;
(c) production can pass through every stage within the period it starts in.

Model 1: Production-inventory planning

Special case of Model 3: Minimum cost network flow in Lecture 4.2

Model 1 formulation: Production-inventory planning

$$
\begin{array}{rrclll}
\mathrlap{\text{Minimize}} & & & & & \\[2pt]
\mathrlap{\qquad \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{t} c_i^p\, x_{ij} + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=2}^{t+1} c_i^i\, y_{ij}} & & & & & \\[16pt]
\mathrlap{\text{subject to}} & & & & & \\[8pt]
& -x_{ij} + x_{(i+1)j} - y_{ij} + y_{i(j+1)} & = & 0, & i = 1, \dots, m-1 & (a) \\[-2pt]
& & & & j = 1, \dots, t & \\[8pt]
& -x_{mj} - y_{mj} + y_{m(j+1)} & = & -d_j, & j = 1, \dots, t & (b) \\[8pt]
& x_{ij} & \le & u_{ij}, & i = 1, \dots, m & (c) \\[-2pt]
& & & & j = 1, \dots, t & \\[8pt]
& y_{i1} & = & y_i^0, & \hphantom{j}\mathllap{i} = 1, \dots, m & (d) \\[8pt]
& y_{i(t+1)} & = & y_i^{t+1}, & \hphantom{j}\mathllap{i} = 1, \dots, m & (d) \\[8pt]
& y_{ij} & \le & u_i^y, & i = 1, \dots, m & (e) \\[-2pt]
& & & & j = 2, \dots, t & \\[8pt]
& x_{ij},\ y_{ij} & \ge & 0 & &
\end{array}
\tag{1}
$$

where

- $x_{ij}$ = production at stage $i$ in period $j$ (ton)
- $y_{ij}$ = inventory at stage $i$ carried from period $j-1$ to period $j$ (ton)
- $c_i^p$ = production cost at stage $i$ (\$/ton)
- $c_i^i$ = inventory cost at stage $i$ (\$/ton-period)
= $h\,(c_1^p + c_2^p + \cdots + c_i^p)$
- $h$ = inventory carrying rate per period (\$/\$-period)
- $d_j$ = demand in period $j$ (ton)
- $u_{ij}$ = capacity of stage $i$ in period $j$ (ton)
- $u_i^y$ = storage capacity at stage $i$ (ton)
- $y_i^0$ = initial inventory at stage $i$ (ton)
- $y_i^{t+1}$ = final inventory at stage $i$ (ton)
- $m$ = number of production stages
- $t$ = number of periods in the planning horizon.

Both lines labeled (d) in Eq. 1 are row (d) on purpose: one constraint, the inventory given at the start and at the end of the horizon.

In the objective function, inventory costs are summed from 2 to $t + 1$ because the period 1 initial inventory cost was accounted for in period 0 prior to period 1 (rolling horizon). Constraints (a) and (b) in the model are the flow-balance equations for each node, while the remaining constraints represent lower- and upper-bounds on the decision variables $x$ and $y$.

The inventory sum in the objective runs from 2 to $t + 1$ for a reason. There are $t + 1$ inventory variables at each stage, four in the three periods of Fig. 1, but summing their costs from 1 to $t + 1$ would double count. In a rolling horizon, this month’s plan carries those four, and next month’s cuts off the first period, adds one at the end, and solves the same model again. With the cost counted every month, the inventory carried from one plan into the next would appear in both, as the final inventory of one and the initial inventory of the other, and over time the plans would show an inventory cost that is not actually incurred. Leaving out the cost of the initial inventory avoids that double counting. The final inventory could have been left out instead, and the initial included: one or the other, but not both. That is an important aspect of these models, and it is why they are written with indices rather than set notation. After the objective function, the model is just flow balance: at every stage but the last, everything sums to zero. The only exception is the last stage, whose sum equals the negative of the demand, because in the net supply formulation of the minimum cost network flow problem a demand is a negative net supply. So Model 1 is another example of the minimum cost network flow problem of Lecture 4.2, a specialization of it.

Because of the need to sum over different portions of the data, indices are used in place of set notation in production-inventory planning models; for example, while $j \in T$ could be used in place of $j = 1, \dots, t$, it would be difficult to use set notation to represent $i = 1, \dots, m-1$.

The flow-balance constraints are the only constraints in the model because the capacity constraints are handled as upper bounds on $x_{ij}$.

Model 1 implementation: Production-inventory planning

```julia
# Model: production-inventory planning
using JuMP, HiGHS, Logjam
function prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d, u, LBʸ, UBʸ)
    m, t = length(cᵖ), length(d)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, 0 ≤ x[i=1:m, j=1:t] ≤ u[i,j])              # (c)
    @variable(model, LBʸ[i,j] ≤ y[i=1:m, j=1:t+1] ≤ UBʸ[i,j])
    @objective(model, Min,
        sum(cᵖ[i]*x[i,j] for i=1:m, j=1:t) +
        sum(cⁱ[i]*y[i,j] for i=1:m, j=2:t+1))
    @constraint(model, flowbal[i=1:m-1, j=1:t],                 # (a)
        -x[i,j] + x[i+1,j] - y[i,j] + y[i,j+1] == 0)
    @constraint(model, laststage[j=1:t],                        # (b)
        -x[m,j] - y[m,j] + y[m,j+1] == -d[j])

    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    if termination_status(model) == JuMP.OPTIMAL
        return (TC = objective_value(model), x = snapvals(value.(x)),
                y = snapvals(value.(y)))
    end
    error(termination_status(model))
end

```

- 1 Rows (d) and (e) are bounds on y: its lower bound LBʸ and upper bound UBʸ are the same initial inventory in period 1 and the same final inventory in period $t + 1$, which fixes both, and between them zero and the storage capacity.

```text
prodinv (generic function with 1 method)
```

### 2.2 Greedy procedure

Inventory costs more to carry at each later stage, because more has been spent producing the product by then, so it often makes sense to carry inventory at an early stage, such as stage 1, and to produce each ton only when it is actually needed.

For a single product, something like a simple greedy procedure can be used, because the network is essentially feed forward, and solving the problem as a linear program can be overkill.

Every arc of the time-expanded network points forward, to a later period or to the next stage, so a plan can be found by working back along it, from the last stage: the last stage’s latest plan leaves every earlier stage the most time to supply it. Model 2 states the procedure, which is how a plan is found by hand. It is a feasibility model, not an optimization model, in the terms of the Model Format Reference: it determines the production with no preference among the plans that work, so it has no objective function, and nothing in it is chosen by cost: under its assumption (a), the production cost is the same for every plan that satisfies the demand, which leaves only the inventory cost, and under the rest, producing each ton as late as capacity allows is what keeps that least. The rule takes the place of the objective, and Ex. 1 checks that its plan costs what the linear program’s does.

solve for:
(a) production at each stage in each period.

subject to:
(a) as late as possible: each stage produces its requirement in the latest periods its capacity allows, the last stage’s requirement being the demand and each other stage’s the production of the stage after it;
(b) initial and final inventory: a stage’s initial inventory meets its earliest requirements, and its final inventory is produced as late as the rest.

assumptions:
(a) production cost and inventory cost per ton at each stage are the same in every period;
(b) inventory cost does not decrease from one stage to the next;
(c) no storage limit binds;
(d) production can pass through every stage within the period it starts in.

Model 2: Greedy as-late-as-possible procedure

Model 2 formulation: Greedy as-late-as-possible procedure

```text
algorithm latestplan;
{ input:  capacities uᵢⱼ, demands dⱼ, initial and final inventories    }
{         y⁰ᵢ and yᵢᵗ⁺¹, stages i = 1 … m, periods j = 1 … t           }
{ output: production xᵢⱼ, or infeasible                                }
begin
    rⱼ := dⱼ, j = 1 … t;                 { the last stage's requirement }
    for i := m downto 1 do
    begin
        meet r₁, r₂, … in turn from y⁰ᵢ, and let s be what is left;
        c := yᵢᵗ⁺¹ − s;                  { final inventory still to make }
        if c < 0 then return infeasible;
        for j := t downto 1 do
        begin
            xᵢⱼ := min(uᵢⱼ, rⱼ + c);
            c := rⱼ + c − xᵢⱼ;           { left to an earlier period }
        end;
        if c > 0 then return infeasible;
        rⱼ := xᵢⱼ, j = 1 … t;            { what stage i − 1 must supply }
    end;
    return x;
end;
```

Model 2 implementation: Greedy as-late-as-possible procedure

```julia
# Model: greedy as-late-as-possible procedure
function latestplan(d, u, y⁰, yᵗ⁺¹)
    m, t = size(u)
    x, r = zeros(m, t), Float64.(d)       # the last stage's requirement
    for i in m:-1:1
        s = Float64(y⁰[i])
        for j in 1:t                       # initial inventory first
            use = min(s, r[j])
            r[j] -= use
            s -= use
        end
        c = yᵗ⁺¹[i] - s                    # final inventory still to make
        c < 0 && return nothing
        for j in t:-1:1                    # as late as possible
            x[i, j] = min(u[i, j], r[j] + c)
            c = r[j] + c - x[i, j]         # left to an earlier period
        end
        c > 0 && return nothing
        r = x[i, :]                        # what stage i - 1 must supply
    end
    y = [y⁰ zeros(m, t)]                   # inventory, by flow balance
    for j in 1:t, i in 1:m
        y[i, j+1] = y[i, j] + x[i, j] - (i < m ? x[i+1, j] : d[j])
    end
    return (x = x, y = y)
end
```

```text
latestplan (generic function with 1 method)
```

Example 1: Two stages with unavailable capacity

For the product of Fig. 1, made in two stages over three months, determine the production plan that minimizes total production and inventory cost, and the cost: by hand, and with Model 1 in Julia.

A single product is produced in two stages. The planning period is three months, and the model is run each month using current demand forecasts and scheduled production capacity. In some periods, the capacity is input as zero, which indicates that it will be used for other purposes during that period. Fig. 1 shows the production-inventory planning network.

Assuming an annual inventory carrying rate of 0.3 \$/\$-yr, the monthly rate is $h = 0.3/12$. The inventory cost per ton at stage $i$ is then the monthly rate times the cumulative cost to produce each ton from stage 1 through $i$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_1^i &= \frac{0.3}{12}\, 200 = 5 \\
c_2^i &= \frac{0.3}{12} \bigl( 200 + 800 \bigr) = 25
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

Eq. 2 is the Units check of Lecture 1.2 at work: a carrying rate in \$/\$-yr becomes an inventory cost in \$/ton-month only once it is divided by 12 months a year and multiplied by a cumulative cost in \$/ton.

Example 1(a): By hand

Determine the plan and its cost by hand, from the capacities and flow balance.

With no inventory at stage 2 at the start or wanted at the end, and no capacity at stage 2 after the first period, all of stage 2’s production has to be in the first period. Can a ton be moved from stage 1 to stage 2 within the same period? It can: a ton can be produced at stage 1 and passed on to stage 2 in the same period, going all the way through, from raw material to finished product, within one period, and nothing forces a wait between the stages. If a stage did have to wait for the next period, the network would have a diagonal arc from stage 1 in one period to stage 2 in the next, and a process taking two months, such as some continuous processes, would have an arc spanning two periods. Networks like that very quickly get complex, but the network remains the best way to visualize them, and about the only one. The problem is also easy to make infeasible. Here all of the production has to be in the first period, where stage 1 can produce 50 tons; the total demand is less than 50 tons, but with a total demand over 50 the plan would not be feasible. That is one of the uses of these models: when demand is high, an infeasible model shows that the operation as it stands does not have the capacity, and that perhaps overtime should be scheduled. Identifying what causes the infeasibility shows what has to change to make the model feasible.

By Model 2, the last stage first, stage 2 produces all three months’ demand in the first month, the only month it has capacity, $x_{2,1} = 20 + 10 + 15 = 45$ tons, and carries $y_{2,2} = 45 - 20 = 25$ tons into month 2 and $y_{2,3} = 25 - 10 = 15$ tons into month 3. Stage 1 feeds it in the same month, $x_{1,1} = 45$ tons, within its capacity of 50. Stage 1’s final inventory of 35 tons can be produced only in month 1, where 5 tons of capacity are left, or in month 3; produced in month 3, it is carried no month before the end of the horizon, so $x_{1,3} = 35$ tons, carried out as $y_{1,4} = 35$. Every other flow is zero, and the cost is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{production:}\quad & 200\,(45 + 35) + 800\,(45) = 52{,}000 \\
\text{inventory:}\quad & 25\,(25 + 15) + 5\,(35) = 1{,}175 \\
\text{total:}\quad & 52{,}000 + 1{,}175 = 53{,}175
\end{aligned}

$$

The final inventory’s cost, $5 \times 35$, is counted because the inventory sum of Eq. 1 runs to $j = t + 1$.

Produce 45 tons at each stage in month 1 and 35 tons at stage 1 in month 3, at a total cost of \$53,175.

Example 1(b): In Julia

Determine the plan and its cost with Model 1.

Code block 2 enters the data of Fig. 1:

```julia
# Code block 2: Ex. 1's data
u = [50  0 50;                # capacity of stage i in period j (ton)
     60  0  0];
d = [20, 10, 15]              # demand in period j (ton)
cᵖ = [200, 800]               # production cost in stage i ($/ton)
h = 0.3/12                    # monthly inventory carrying rate (1/month)
@show cⁱ = cumsum(cᵖ)*h       # inventory cost for stage i ($/ton)
y⁰ = [0, 0]                   # initial inventory of stage i (ton)
yᵗ⁺¹ = [35, 0]                # final inventory of stage i (ton)
m = length(cᵖ)                # number of production stages = 2
t = length(d)                 # number of periods of production = 3
LBʸ = [y⁰ zeros(m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹] # same LB and UB to fix inventory level
UBʸ = [y⁰ fill(Inf, m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹];
```

```text
cⁱ = cumsum(cᵖ) * h = [5.0, 24.999999999999996]
```

The printed inventory costs are where the 5 and the 25 of Fig. 1 come from. The initial inventory is 0 at both stages and the final inventory 35 and 0, taken from the figure. The number of production stages, m, is the number of elements in the production cost, and the number of periods, t, the length of the demand vector, rather than being hard-coded, so that a change in the number of stages or periods changes them too. The lower and upper bounds on inventory, LBʸ and UBʸ, are both the initial inventory, y⁰, in their first column; between it and the last column the lower bound is zero, since inventory need not be carried, and in this problem the upper bound is infinity. Setting the lower and upper bounds to the same value clamps the inventory: it forces the variable to have that value. The final inventory, in the last column, is forced the same way, both bounds set to it. Those are all the inputs the model needs, and solving it is much like solving the minimum cost network flow problem, an application of what has already been seen.

The 25 prints as 24.999999999999996 because 0.3/12 has no exact binary representation, a rounding far too small to matter. Logjam’s snapvals, which Model 1’s implementation applies to its solution, rounds a value that close to a whole number to it: snapvals(cⁱ) is [5.0, 25.0].

Code block 3 solves Ex. 1 with the implementation of Model 1, in place of a model written out for the example, and again with Model 2’s, which needs no solver:

```julia

TCᵒ, xᵒ, yᵒ = prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d, u, LBʸ, UBʸ)
@show TCᵒ
xˡ, yˡ = latestplan(d, u, y⁰, yᵗ⁺¹)
@show sum(cᵖ .* xˡ) + sum(cⁱ .* yˡ[:, 2:end]);   # its cost

```

- 1 prodinv returns a named tuple, (TC = …, x = …, y = …), and assigning it to three names unpacks its fields in order, so TCᵒ, xᵒ and yᵒ hold the total cost, the production and the inventory.
- 2 Model 2 finds the plan a second way, without a solver, and its cost should match TCᵒ: two routes to one number, a validation, the Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2.

Stage 1, with a capacity of 50 tons in the first month, produces 45 tons then and carries no inventory, and stage 2 carries 25 tons of inventory into the second month and 15 into the third. Everything balances. At stage 1 in the first month, 0 tons come in as inventory and 45 are produced, while 0 go out as inventory and 45 go on to stage 2, so the node nets to zero. At stage 2, 0 tons come in as inventory and 45 are produced, and 25 go out as inventory, so the node nets 20 tons out, the demand. Every node nets to zero except those of the last stage, which net to the demand: the plan is just a set of accounting identities that have to hold. NoteEx. 1 as a minimum cost network flow

As a minimum cost network flow, Model 3 in Lecture 4.2, the network of Fig. 1 needs a node for each arc to start from: a supply node feeding stage 1 in every period, and for each stage a node holding its initial inventory and a node receiving its final inventory. The last stage’s nodes are the demand nodes, each with the period’s demand as a negative net supply, and every other node is a transshipment node. Each production arc is bounded by its capacity, and the inventory arcs between periods are unbounded. Code block 7 repeats Lecture 4.2’s implementation of the model:

```julia
# Code block 7: list2incid and mcnf, as implemented in Lecture 4.2
using SparseArrays
list2incid(i, j, n) = sparse([i; j], [1:length(i); 1:length(i)],
                             [ones(length(i)); -ones(length(j))],
                             n, length(i))

function mcnf(A, c, s; u = fill(Inf, size(A, 2)), l = zeros(size(A, 2)))
    V, E = 1:size(A, 1), 1:size(A, 2)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, l[k] ≤ x[k ∈ E] ≤ u[k])                  # (b)
    @objective(model, Min, sum(c[k] * x[k] for k ∈ E))
    @constraint(model, supply[i ∈ V; s[i] > 0],
                sum(A[i, k] * x[k] for k ∈ E) ≤ s[i])               # (a)
    @constraint(model, balance[i ∈ V; s[i] ≤ 0],
                sum(A[i, k] * x[k] for k ∈ E) == s[i])              # (a)

    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    if termination_status(model) == JuMP.OPTIMAL
        return (TC = objective_value(model), x = snapvals(value.(x)))
    end
    error(termination_status(model))
end
```

```text
mcnf (generic function with 1 method)
```

The initial inventory arcs cost nothing, because their cost was already incurred in the previous period; the final ones cost $c_i^i$, as the inventory sum of Eq. 1 runs from $j = 2$ to $t + 1$. Code block 8 builds the network’s arc list from Ex. 1’s data, production arcs first, period by period, and then each stage’s inventory arcs, solves the network, and compares its production arcs, the first $mt$ in the list, with Ex. 1(b)’s plan:

```julia
# Code block 8: Ex. 1's time-expanded network as an arc list, solved
# Node 1 supplies stage 1; node nd(i, j) is stage i in period j; then a
# node per stage for its initial inventory, and one for its final
nd(i, j) = 1 + (j - 1)*m + i
B(i) = 1 + m*t + i
F(i) = 1 + m*t + m + i
n = 1 + m*t + 2m
I, J, c, ub, lb = Int[], Int[], Float64[], Float64[], Float64[]
arc!(a, b, cc, uu, ll = 0.0) = (push!(I, a); push!(J, b); push!(c, cc);
                                push!(ub, uu); push!(lb, ll))
for j in 1:t, i in 1:m                        # production
    arc!(i == 1 ? 1 : nd(i - 1, j), nd(i, j), cᵖ[i], u[i, j])
end
for i in 1:m
    arc!(B(i), nd(i, 1), 0.0, y⁰[i], y⁰[i])          # initial inventory
    for j in 1:t-1
        arc!(nd(i, j), nd(i, j + 1), cⁱ[i], Inf)      # inventory
    end
    arc!(nd(i, t), F(i), cⁱ[i], yᵗ⁺¹[i], yᵗ⁺¹[i])     # final inventory
end
s = zeros(n)                                  # net supplies
s[1] = sum(d) + sum(yᵗ⁺¹)                     # enough for any plan
for i in 1:m
    s[B(i)], s[F(i)] = y⁰[i], -yᵗ⁺¹[i]
end
for j in 1:t
    s[nd(m, j)] = -d[j]
end
@show length(I)                               # arcs
@show n                                       # nodes
TCᵐ, xᵐ = mcnf(list2incid(I, J, n), c, s; u = ub, l = lb)
@show TCᵐ
reshape(xᵐ[1:m*t], m, t) == xᵒ                # the plan of Ex. 1(b)

```

- 1 Each call appends one arc to the list: start node, end node, cost, upper bound and lower bound (0 unless given). Giving the initial and final inventory arcs the same lower and upper bound fixes their flow, as LBʸ and UBʸ do in Model 1’s implementation.

### 2.3 Flows determined by flow balance

Flow balance makes it possible to determine some of the flows in a production-inventory network by hand. Given a diagram of the network with only some of its flows, the missing flows are filled in from the flow balance at its nodes. Doing so is a good way of demonstrating an understanding of the basic structure of these networks.

Missing flows are not something to expect in practice, and filling them in is not part of the normal use of these models. Where some are missing, this is a way to fill them in; it works only because the structure of the model is such that some of the data can be determined from the rest. It is brought up here because it is a useful way of testing an understanding of that structure. Were flows to be found to any large extent, it would be coded up, so that the model determined them automatically. Exs. 2 and 3 are two such tests, the first with one flow missing and the second with data of several kinds missing.

Example 2: One missing flow

Determine the missing value of flow c in the network of Fig. 3(a).

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 9: Ex. 2's network as given, and its missing flow found
# frame! draws the flows N on the network, each marked by what it is in
# N₀, the network as given: given red, unknown black and named, found blue
# and named; a node in hl is circled in blue. A flow is named by its array
# and indices: (:X, i, j) production, (:Y, i, j) inventory, (:d, j) demand
function frame!(ax, N, N₀, name; hl = [], r = 0.16, ls = 12)
    m, t = size(N.X)
    hidedecorations!(ax); hidespines!(ax)
    P(i, j) = ((j - 1) * 1.7, -(i - 1) * 1.6)     # stage i, period j
    arc(p, q) = arrows2d!(ax, [p[1]], [p[2]], [q[1] - p[1]],
                          [q[2] - p[2]]; color = ink, shaftwidth = 1.0,
                          tipwidth = 6, tiplength = 6)
    function lab(k)                               # a flow's label, color
        v, v₀ = N[k[1]][k[2:end]...], N₀[k[1]][k[2:end]...]
        ismissing(v₀) || return string(v₀), datac
        s = rich(it(name[k]), up(ismissing(v) ? " = ?" : " = $v"))
        return s, ismissing(v) ? ink : flowc
    end
    tx(p, k, al) = ((s, c) = lab(k); text!(ax, p[1], p[2]; text = s,
                    color = c, fontsize = ls, align = al))
    for j in 1:t                                  # production and demand
        x0, y0 = P(1, j)
        arc((x0, y0 + 0.9), (x0, y0 + r))
        tx((x0 + 0.08, y0 + 0.5), (:X, 1, j), (:left, :center))
        for i in 2:m
            p, q = P(i - 1, j), P(i, j)
            arc(p .- (0, r), q .+ (0, r))
            tx((p[1] + 0.08, (p[2] + q[2]) / 2), (:X, i, j),
               (:left, :center))
        end
        xm, ym = P(m, j)
        arc((xm, ym - r), (xm, ym - 0.7))
        tx((xm, ym - 0.8), (:d, j), (:center, :top))
    end
    for i in 1:m                                  # inventory
        p = P(i, 1) .- (0.75, 0)
        arc(p, P(i, 1) .- (r, 0))
        tx(p .- (0.08, 0), (:Y, i, 1), (:right, :center))
        for j in 1:t-1
            p, q = P(i, j) .+ (r, 0), P(i, j + 1) .- (r, 0)
            arc(p, q)
            tx(((p[1] + q[1]) / 2, p[2] + 0.12), (:Y, i, j + 1),
               (:center, :bottom))
        end
        q = P(i, t) .+ (0.75, 0)
        arc(P(i, t) .+ (r, 0), q)
        tx(q .+ (0.08, 0), (:Y, i, t + 1), (:left, :center))
    end
    for i in 1:m, j in 1:t                        # nodes, over the arcs
        h = (i, j) in hl
        poly!(ax, Circle(Point2f(P(i, j)...), r); color = :white,
              strokecolor = h ? flowc : ink, strokewidth = h ? 2.6 : 1.4)
    end
    xlims!(ax, -1.45, 5.3); ylims!(ax, -2.85, 1.0)
    return ax
end

X = [9 0 19; 19 0 12]                 # production at stage i in period j
d = [7, 12, 8]                        # demand in period j

     0  missing 0 4]                  #   j, missing where unknown
Yᵒ = copy(Y)
Yᵒ[2, 2] = Y[2, 1] + X[2, 1] - d[1]   # flow balance at stage 2, month 1
N₀ = (X = X, Y = Y, d = d)

        (N, [(2, 1)], "(b) Balance at stage 2, month 1")])

end
```

Figure 3: Ex. 2’s missing flow found by flow balance: (a) the network as given, its production, demand and inventory flows in red and the unknown inventory flow $c$; (b) the node of stage 2 in month 1 balanced, circled in blue, and the flow it determines in blue.

At stage 2 in the first month, 19 tons come in, and 7 are needed for the demand, which leaves 12, and the only place the 12 can go is into the second month as inventory, so c is 12; every other node nets the rest to zero. Flow balance always holds, so it is a way of validating, whenever a plan has any complexity, that things are working the way they should: the Balance check of Lecture 1.2.

$c$ = 12.

NoteFind missing flows using Julia

Code block 10 finds missing flows the way they are found by hand, node by node: fillflows balances each node that has exactly one unknown flow, records the step, and repeats until no flow is missing. Production $x_{ij}$ is the matrix X, inventory $y_{ij}$ the matrix Y, and demand $d_j$ the vector d, each with missing for an unknown, and the flows found are returned in N:

```julia
# Code block 10: missing flows found node by node by flow balance
# At node (i, j), inventory in plus production equals what goes on, to
# stage i + 1 or to demand, plus inventory out; a node with one unknown
# flow determines it, and each step records the node and the flow found
function fillflows(X, Y, d)
    m, t = size(X)
    N = (X = copy(X), Y = copy(Y), d = copy(d))
    v(k) = N[k[1]][k[2:end]...]
    steps = Tuple[]
    while any(A -> any(ismissing, A), N)
        n = length(steps)
        for i in 1:m, j in 1:t
            F = [(+1, (:Y, i, j)), (+1, (:X, i, j)),           # in
                 (-1, i < m ? (:X, i + 1, j) : (:d, j)),       # on
                 (-1, (:Y, i, j + 1))]                         # out
            u = [f for f in F if ismissing(v(f[2]))]
            length(u) == 1 || continue
            s, k = u[1]
            N[k[1]][k[2:end]...] =
                -s * sum(s′ * v(k′) for (s′, k′) in F if k′ != k)
            push!(steps, (i, j, k))
        end
        length(steps) > n || error("flow balance cannot find the rest")
    end
    return N, steps
end

X = [9 0 19; 19 0 12]                 # production at stage i in period j
d = [7, 12, 8]                        # demand in period j
Y = [10 0       0 7;                  # inventory at stage i into period
     0  missing 0 4]                  #   j, missing where unknown
N, steps = fillflows(X, Y, d)
@show steps
N.Y[2, 2]

```

- 1 A flow is named by its array and its indices, (:Y, 2, 2) for $y_{2,2}$, (:X, 1, 3) for $x_{1,3}$ and (:d, 1) for $d_1$, and v(k) reads the flow named k.
- 2 The unknown flow’s sign s is $+1$ if it comes into the node and $-1$ if it goes out. Flow balance, what comes in less what goes out equal to zero, gives the flow as $-s$ times the signed sum of the node’s other three.
- 3 n counts the steps before a pass. If a pass finds nothing, the rest cannot be found by flow balance alone, and the error says so.

Not every result is needed to know the plan. In Ex. 1, if the other three flows at stage 1 in month 3 are known, the only possible result for its production is the 35 tons, because every node except those of the last stage has to net to zero: whatever comes in has to go out. The only difference at the last stage is the demand that has to be satisfied.

The flows behave like water flowing through a pipe, and the analogy is exact. With some of the information missing, the rest can be inferred from these two ideas, which is how the problem is done by hand.

Figure 4: Ex. 3’s missing data found by flow balance, one frame per step of fillflows (Code block 10): (a) the network as given, its known flows in red and four unknowns, the production flow $p$, the inventory flow $q$, the final inventory $r$ and the demand $s$; (b) to (e) one node balanced at each step, circled in blue, and the value it determines in blue; (f) the two nodes left over, which balance too.

Stage 1 is balanced first, month by month. In month 1, the 10 tons of initial inventory and the 40 produced come in, and 25 are carried into month 2, so what goes on to stage 2 is $p = 10 + 40 - 25 = 25$ (frame b). In month 2, the 25 carried in and nothing produced feed the 20 that stage 2 makes, which leaves $q = 25 + 0 - 20 = 5$ to carry into month 3 (frame c). In month 3, those 5 and the 30 produced feed the 22 that stage 2 makes, which leaves the final inventory, $r = 5 + 30 - 22 = 13$ (frame d), so $r$ could be found only after $q$. At stage 2, month 2’s node gives the demand: the 11 carried in and the 20 made, less the 7 carried out, $s = 11 + 20 - 7 = 24$ (frame e). The two nodes left over check the answer (frame f): in month 1, $6 + 25$ comes in and $20 + 11$ goes out, and in month 3, $7 + 22$ comes in and $17 + 12$ goes out. The first of the two is also a second route to $p$, since its only unknown was $p$: $p = 20 + 11 - 6 = 25$, the Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2.

$p$ = 25, $q$ = 5, $r$ = 13, $s$ = 24.

Not all missing variables can be recovered: two unknowns that meet at only one node are known only through their sum, as the demand in month 3 and stage 2’s final inventory would be in Ex. 3, and fillflows then stops with its error.

### 2.4 Limits of the greedy procedure

Example 4: Scheduled maintenance

A single product is produced in a two-stage production process. Stage one has a capacity to produce 40 tons of the product per month, and there is a cost of \$200 for each ton of product produced. For stage two, capacity is 80 tons per month, and there is a cost of \$800 per ton. Due to scheduled maintenance, no capacity will be available during month five for stage 1 and during months three and five for stage 2. Demand for the next six months is estimated to be 25, 15, 10, 50, 25, and 15 tons per month. Currently, five tons of material is in storage at stage 1 and 25 tons at stage 2; at the end of the planning period, ten tons of material should be in storage at stage 1 and 15 at stage 2. Up to 30 tons of material per month can be stored at each stage. Assuming that the inventory costs are \$12 and \$46 per ton-month, determine the production plan that minimizes total costs over the planning horizon and what the total production costs will be, and what the total inventory costs will be.

Solution approach: Can use the Single-Product with Variable Capacity model, Model 1. The maximum inventory storage constraint can be modeled as an upper bound on $y$.

Ex. 4 is how a problem would arise in practice: a description gives the demand, all of the costs and the other data, and reading it translates it into the model’s data. Here there are two stages and six periods, six months, with a demand for each. Stage 2 is shut down in month 3, and both stages in month 5, for scheduled maintenance; otherwise they run at their normal capacities of 40 and 80 tons. Instead of a carrying rate from which to calculate the inventory costs, the inventory costs $c_i^i$ themselves are given, \$12 and \$46 per ton-month, along with the initial and final inventories. What is different from Ex. 1 is that the upper bound on inventory is not infinity: up to 30 tons can be stored at each stage. A limit other than infinity on how much inventory can be held between stages is not unusual: a production system does not have infinite storage, and there may be only a certain buffer for the inventory passed from one stage to the next, so a maximum inventory that can be carried is quite common. With it, the inventory’s bounds are the initial inventory, the final inventory, and an upper bound of 30 tons on every period in between, row (e) of Eq. 1.

```julia
# Code block 12: Ex. 4's data
u = [40 40 40 40 0 40;          # capacity of each stage (ton)
     80 80  0 80 0 80]
d = [25, 15, 10, 50, 25, 15]    # demand in each period (ton)
# variable production cost for each stage ($/ton)
cᵖ = [200, 800]
cⁱ = [12, 46]                   # inventory cost for each stage ($/ton)
y⁰ = [5, 25]                    # initial inventory of each stage (ton)
yᵗ⁺¹ = [10, 15]                 # final inventory of each stage (ton)
m = length(cᵖ)                  # number of production stages
t = length(d)                   # number of periods of production
# same LB and UB to fix initial and final inventory levels
LBʸ = [y⁰ zeros(m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹]
UBʸ = [y⁰ fill(30, m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹];  # max inventory storage level
```

Negative zeros, and values that are really close to zero, are fixed by snapping each value to the closest integer when it is really close, since it is typically supposed to be an integer value, with an absolute tolerance of $10^{-8}$. Logjam’s snapvals does this.

Code block 13 solves it with Model 1’s implementation, which reads every value through snapvals, as in Lecture 2.7. It then tries Model 2, whose assumption (c) the storage limit puts in doubt, and solves the problem once more without the limit:

```julia
# Code block 13: Ex. 4 solved with prodinv, and as late as possible
TCᵒ, xᵒ, yᵒ = prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d, u, LBʸ, UBʸ)
@show TCᵒ
xˡ, yˡ = latestplan(d, u, y⁰, yᵗ⁺¹)
TCˡ = sum(cᵖ .* xˡ) + sum(cⁱ .* yˡ[:, 2:end])   # its cost
@show TCˡ
@show maximum(yˡ[:, 2:t])          # the most it holds at a stage
UBⁿ = [y⁰ fill(Inf, m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹]  # no storage limit
@show prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d, u, LBʸ, UBⁿ).TC;
```

```text
TCᵒ = 134300.0
TCˡ = 133900.0
maximum(yˡ[:, 2:t]) = 35.0
(prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d, u, LBʸ, UBⁿ)).TC = 133900.0
```

The latest plan carries 35 tons at stage 1 into month 4, built ahead for the 75 tons stage 2 makes in month 4, that month’s demand and the next one’s, when stage 2 is down, which is more than stage 1 can make in one month; and 35 tons is more than the 30 a stage can store. Without the limit it would be optimal, at \$133,900, the cost of the linear program with the limit removed; with the limit, the linear program holds part of the build-ahead at stage 2 instead, where it costs more to carry, and its plan costs \$400 more. A storage limit is where the procedure stops being enough.

Code blocks 16 to 19 are a sanity check, a way of making sure that a model is doing its accounting correctly, and the way the need to include the initial or the final inventory, but not both, comes to light. The total production cost and the total inventory cost are calculated from the plan, added up, and compared with the model’s objective. Summed over every inventory arc, they come to \$135,510, more than the model’s \$134,300, because the model excludes the first period. Recalculated from period 2, the inventory cost is \$3,300 rather than \$4,510, and the sum then equals the objective. For any moderately complex production-inventory problem, this bookkeeping check is worth doing almost always: whatever the model reports as its objective is recalculated from its plan, to make sure it can be duplicated. It is a great way of catching any errors that creep into the calculation, and it is the Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2, two routes to one number.

Total cost \$134,300: production \$131,000 and inventory \$3,300.

A stage can have more than one resource. Between two nodes of the network there can then be two arcs, a multigraph, as when there are two transport options; even for a single product, one stage of production can be the transportation of the product rather than production as such, with a base transport option and a costlier overflow option. The same holds for production proper: a base machine, and, for excess production, a secondary machine that is more expensive to run but is available for overflow. That is the way an electric utility serves its demand, and it is a valuable way of looking at these problems. An electric utility typically has base load units, typically nuclear and coal units, and gas turbines, for example, that handle the peak demands. The idea is used throughout production systems as a way of handling variability in demand.

In such a multigraph the base unit typically has an upper bound, and the more expensive alternative is needed only for a demand that exceeds it. Ex. 6(d) in Lecture 4.2 is the example: the cheaper of two modes carries at most 20 units, and only what it cannot carry takes the costlier one. Overtime is such a costlier resource: it is what Ex. 1(a) suggests scheduling when a plan comes back infeasible because the operation, as it stands, does not have the capacity.

## 3. Capacity determined inside the model

Even where capacity is set to zero and the decision is made outside the model, it is still quite hard for a person to look at all the different trade-offs once the number of stages and periods gets long enough. Table 1 summarizes the single-product problems of this lecture by what it takes to solve each: when a simple greedy procedure solves the problem, when it is a linear program that the greedy procedure cannot solve, when it requires dynamic programming, and when it requires more. It also motivates the mixed-integer linear programming version of the problem, as a way of internalizing the need to make these decisions. In Sec. 2, the indicator that gates the capacity is provided outside the model.

Table 1: Single-product problems in this lecture: whether capacity’s availability is set outside the model or gated inside it, whether production carries a setup cost, and what solves each.

| Capacity | Problem | Solved by |
|---|---|---|
| Set outside the model: $u_{ij}$ given, $0$ where unavailable | no setup cost, Model 2’s assumptions hold (Exs. 1, 7) | greedy procedure, Model 2, at the linear program’s cost |
| | no setup cost, a storage limit binds (Ex. 4) | linear program, Model 1; the greedy plan breaks the limit |
| | no setup cost, a base resource and a costlier one, a multigraph (Sec. 2.4) | minimum cost network flow on the multigraph, as in Lecture 4.2 |
| Gated inside the model by indicators $z_{ij}$ | no setup cost (Sec. 3) | linear program, Model 1: the indicators determine nothing |
| | setup cost, one stage, no capacity limit (Sec. 3 note) | dynamic program of Wagner and Whitin |
| | setup cost, stages with capacity (Exs. 5, 6) | mixed-integer linear program, Model 3 |

The indicator gates capacity in row (c) of Eq. 3 below, $x_{ij} \le u_i z_{ij}$, and the setup cost puts it in the objective, as $c_i^s z_{ij}$.

Two costs do not vary with the amount produced, a switchover cost and a setup cost. A switchover cost is incurred when production switches from one product to another; as long as the same product continues to be produced in the next period, there is no additional cost. A setup cost is the estimated cost of setting up to produce a product in a period. Neither is the “fixed cost” of the Location lectures, the intercept of a regression line fitted to production costs (Lecture 2.4, Sec. 8), and that fixed cost does not carry over to production-inventory planning, because production-inventory planning is primarily a tactical problem. Location is strategic: its production cost is an aggregate, and fitting a regression to capture economies of scale makes sense there. Here a period can be as short as a week or a day, too short for economies of scale, and a product made period after period would be charged the intercept again in every period. A regression’s intercept is appropriate only for strategic problems whose period is a year or more.

Most of the time, the cost of operating and producing in a period is mostly a variable cost, a constant applied to the units produced in the period. What takes the model from a linear program to a mixed-integer linear program is a setup cost in a period, assumed to be incurred in each period in which a resource produces: literally getting the machine up and running, for example, a cost independent of how much is produced but incurred every period.

In some situations, though, the setup cost is nearly everything. A truckload is one: between two points, most of its cost is independent of the load carried, up to the truck’s maximum payload, which is why Ex. 6 treats a truck as a setup.

A setup that does not have to be repeated each period is a switchover. For a single product its cost is incurred once, at the very beginning, whatever plan is made, so from a modeling point of view it can be ignored; switchover costs matter once there are several products to switch among (Lecture 4.4). Setup costs recur, each shift say, as in the validation or calibration of equipment.

A setup cost needs a variable that says whether a stage produces in a period: a binary variable $z$, called an indicator variable, a kind of variable used in several contexts, 1 if the stage produces in the period and 0 otherwise. Added to the objective function, it incurs the setup cost whenever the stage produces. Even with a single product, a large setup cost can change the decision: where the linear program would produce a small quantity in some month, the setup cost, independent of the quantity, can make it optimal not to produce at that stage that month, and to produce a little more earlier, carrying it as inventory, or a little later. Which periods to produce in is then determined by the model, through its indicator variables, rather than by the person running it, as the zero capacities of Sec. 2 required.

The number of truckloads in a week is not restricted to one, and typically there is no reason to restrict it: one dedicated truck making round trips might take all week, but in practice a third-party trucking company can send one, two or a dozen trucks at any time. So the number of trucks is an integer variable rather than a binary one, and the setup cost is incurred for however many truckloads are sent.

Model 3 generalizes Model 1 with the number of setups at each stage in each period. A machine is set up at most once in a period, so for a machine the number is the indicator; for trucks it is a count.

minimize: total production, inventoryand setup cost over the planning horizon

solve for:
(a) production at each stage in each period;
(b) inventory at each stage carried into each period;
(c) number of setups at each stage in each period.

subject to:
(a) flow balance at each stage that feeds the next: what is produced or carried in is either passed on to the next stage or carried out;
(b) flow balance at the last stage, which feeds demand: what is produced or carried in either meets the period’s demand or is carried out;
(c) capacity: production at each stage in each period is no more than its capacityper setup times its number of setups;
(d) initial and final inventory: inventory at each stage at the start and at the end of the horizon is given;
(e) storage: inventory at each stage between periods is no more than its storage capacity.

assumptions:
(a) production cost and inventory cost per ton at each stage are constant;
(b) demand in each period is given;
(c) production can pass through every stage within the period it starts in;
(d) setup cost is incurred for each setup at a stage, whatever the setup then produces;
(e) inventory carries each ton’s share of its setups, taken at a full setup’s capacity.

Model 3: Production-inventory with setups

Generalization of Model 1: Production-inventory planning

Model 3 formulation: Production-inventory with setups

$$
\begin{array}{rrclll}
\mathrlap{\text{Minimize}} & & & & & \\[2pt]
\mathrlap{\qquad \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=1}^{t} \bigl( c_i^p\, x_{ij} + c_i^s\, z_{ij} \bigr) + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{j=2}^{t+1} c_i^i\, y_{ij}} & & & & & \\[16pt]
\mathrlap{\text{subject to}} & & & & & \\[8pt]
& -x_{ij} + x_{(i+1)j} - y_{ij} + y_{i(j+1)} & = & 0, & i = 1, \dots, m-1 & (a) \\[-2pt]
& & & & j = 1, \dots, t & \\[8pt]
& -x_{mj} - y_{mj} + y_{m(j+1)} & = & -d_j, & j = 1, \dots, t & (b) \\[8pt]
& x_{ij} & \le & u_i\, z_{ij}, & i = 1, \dots, m & (c) \\[-2pt]
& & & & j = 1, \dots, t & \\[8pt]
& y_{i1} & = & y_i^0, & \hphantom{j}\mathllap{i} = 1, \dots, m & (d) \\[8pt]
& y_{i(t+1)} & = & y_i^{t+1}, & \hphantom{j}\mathllap{i} = 1, \dots, m & (d) \\[8pt]
& y_{ij} & \le & u_i^y, & i = 1, \dots, m & (e) \\[-2pt]
& & & & j = 2, \dots, t & \\[8pt]
& x_{ij},\ y_{ij} & \ge & 0 & & \\[8pt]
& z_{ij} & \in & \mathrlap{\{0, 1, \dots, \bar{z}_{ij}\}} & &
\end{array}
\tag{3}
$$

where

- $z_{ij}$ = number of setups at stage $i$ in period $j$
- $c_i^s$ = setup cost at stage $i$ (\$/setup)
- $u_i$ = capacity per setup at stage $i$ (ton/setup)
- $u_i^y$ = storage capacity at stage $i$ (ton)
- $\bar{z}_{ij}$ = most setups at stage $i$ in period $j$
- $c_i^i$ = inventory cost at stage $i$ (\$/ton-period)
= $h\,\bigl[(c_1^p + c_1^s/u_1) + \cdots + (c_i^p + c_i^s/u_i)\bigr]$.

The other symbols are those of Eq. 1. Both lines labeled (d) in Eq. 3 are row (d), as in Eq. 1.

What to use for the inventory cost per period is not obvious once production has a setup cost as well as a cost proportional to the tons produced. The setup cost cannot simply be left out of it, because it can be the most significant cost relative to inventory: in some situations a setup can cost more than the value of the product, being essentially the main production activity, and dropping it would make such situations grossly inaccurate. The setup cost is allocated to the inventory cost at a stage by assumption (e) of Model 3. Each ton is charged a share of every setup it has passed through, the setup cost divided by the capacity per setup, added to the production cost of each stage up to the stage it is at before the carrying rate is applied:

$$
c_i^i = h \left[ \left( c_1^p + \frac{c_1^s}{u_1} \right) + \cdots + \left( c_i^p + \frac{c_i^s}{u_i} \right) \right]
\tag{4}
$$

Using the capacity $u_i$ in the denominator is conservative with respect to the cost allocation, since most stages probably operate below capacity: a setup is then shared by fewer tons than $u_i$, and Eq. 4 charges each ton the smallest share it could carry. It slightly understates the inventory cost, but it includes some part of the setup cost incurred every time a stage produces in a period.

Some inputs are “lumpy,” that is, the cost of utilizing the input is the same over a range of outputs (e.g., the labor costs to set up a machine are the same whether one or 100 parts are produced).

Constraint (c) represents available production capacity and uses the setups $z$ to indicate whether production occurs. The capacity is assumed to be available in discrete units that are either at 100% of the unit’s capacity or not available at all. Integer decision variables are used to make these decisions. This internal capacity decision requires the model to be solved as a MILP.

Producing anything therefore requires a setup, and a setup is paid for in the objective. For a machine, $\bar{z}_{ij}$ is 1 in a period in which it is available and 0 in one in which it is down; for trucks, it is as many as could ever be needed. With no setup costs and machines only, Model 3 is Model 1 with capacities $u_{ij} = u_i\bar{z}_{ij}$.

Time spent setting up a machine when the machine is stopped and can not be operating is termed the machine’s internal setup time; in contrast, the machine’s external setup time is the time required to prepare to produce a particular part on the machine that does not require the machine to be stopped (e.g., fixture preparation). A machine’s “down time” represents the percentage of time the machine is not available for production due to repair or planned maintenance; it does not include internal setup time because the machine is still available for production during this time.

Setup costs are also where Model 2 stops applying,2 and they make the problem far harder to solve.

A mixed-integer linear program like this one would have been hard to solve in the 1980s for a production problem of any realistic size; it was not until the early to mid 1990s that such problems became feasible to solve.

Even a problem like this one with a setup cost, solved in a minute, can change: in a mixed-integer program, changing one number from 100 to 300 can leave the problem feasible but take it from solving in one minute to three hours with the solver, since it is highly nonlinear.

Instead of capacities changed by hand period by period, each stage has a single capacity for all periods, and the indicator variables act like a switch, or a valve, turning that capacity off or on; otherwise the model is essentially the same as before, and with the setup cost allocated to the inventory cost by Eq. 4, everything else carries through as before.

The implementation is almost the same as before. The setups are added to the objective, multiplied by the setup cost, and the capacity, which could be a bound in the definition of the production variable while it was given to the model, becomes a constraint of its own, since it is now determined in the model: the capacity per setup times the setups turns the capacity off or on. In the solution the setups should match the production, zero where nothing is produced and positive where something is: the production gives the amount, and the setups say whether the stage produces in the period. The accounting check is done as before. As a linear program, it was up to the person running the model to work out in which periods to produce; with the setup cost in the model, the model makes that decision itself, and that is the gateway to much more complex decision-making.

Model 3 implementation: Production-inventory with setups

```julia
# Model: production-inventory planning with setup costs
function prodinv_setup(cᵖ, cˢ, cⁱ, d, u, z̄, LBʸ, UBʸ)
    m, t = size(z̄)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, x[i=1:m, j=1:t] ≥ 0)
    @variable(model, 0 ≤ z[i=1:m, j=1:t] ≤ z̄[i,j], Int)
    @variable(model, LBʸ[i,j] ≤ y[i=1:m, j=1:t+1] ≤ UBʸ[i,j])
    @objective(model, Min,
        sum(cᵖ[i]*x[i,j] + cˢ[i]*z[i,j] for i=1:m, j=1:t) +
        sum(cⁱ[i]*y[i,j] for i=1:m, j=2:t+1))
    @constraint(model, flowbal[i=1:m-1, j=1:t],                 # (a)
        -x[i,j] + x[i+1,j] - y[i,j] + y[i,j+1] == 0)
    @constraint(model, laststage[j=1:t],                        # (b)
        -x[m,j] - y[m,j] + y[m,j+1] == -d[j])
    @constraint(model, capacity[i=1:m, j=1:t],                  # (c)
        x[i,j] ≤ u[i]*z[i,j])

    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    if termination_status(model) == JuMP.OPTIMAL
        return (TC = objective_value(model), x = snapvals(value.(x)),
                y = snapvals(value.(y)), z = Int.(snapvals(value.(z))))
    end
    error(termination_status(model))
end

```

- 1 The stages and periods are read from the most setups, z̄[i, j], a matrix laid out like the capacities u[i, j] of Model 1’s implementation; the capacity per setup u is now a vector, one value for each stage.

```text
prodinv_setup (generic function with 1 method)
```

Without the setup cost. Take $c_i^s = 0$ in Eq. 3. The indicator still gates the capacity, row (c), but nothing in the objective makes the model turn it off, so wherever a stage may be set up its capacity is there at no cost: the model is Model 1 with $u_{ij} = u_i\bar{z}_{ij}$, and which periods are available is determined outside it, as in Sec. 2.

For this problem, a single product, there is no easy way of making the decision inside the model without something like a setup cost. Additional constraints could be added to the problem to make the gate determine something, but a model is kept as simple as possible, with elements added only when they are absolutely needed, and adding to the model just to make the decision is extra complexity rather than the problem’s natural state. The setup cost is the natural element: it is what makes producing in a period cost something, and so what makes in which periods to produce a decision for the model.

With several products, the subject of Lecture 4.4, a gate alone does determine something. When a resource is shared exclusively among products, its capacity is turned on or off by the same production indicator, and a linking constraint lets only one product’s indicator be 1 at a stage in a period: one product or the other, not both. The objective function does not include any additional terms. The linking constraint is an additional constraint, with nothing added to the objective function, and everything else flows through as before.

Example 5: Setup costs in manufacturing

A single product is produced in a two-stage production process. Stage one has the capacity to produce 40 tons of the product per month, and there is a setup cost of \$6,000 per month and a variable cost of \$200 for each ton of product produced. For stage two, capacity is 80 tons per month, and there is a setup cost of \$18,000 and a variable cost of \$800. The setup costs are only incurred when any amount of production occurs at that stage for that month. Demand for the next six months is estimated to be 25, 15, 10, 50, 25, and 15 tons per month. Currently, five tons of material are in storage at stage one and 25 tons at stage two; at the end of the planning period, ten tons of material should be in storage at stage one and 15 at stage two. Up to 30 tons of material per month can be stored at each stage. Assuming that the annual inventory carrying rate is 0.4 \$/\$-yr, determine the production plan that minimizes total costs over the planning horizon and what those total costs will be.

Solution approach: Model 3 extends Model 1 with a production indicator binary variable to turn capacity on or off at each stage for each period. One modeling issue is determining inventory cost per ton if the production cost includes a setup cost. An approximation is to allocate the setup cost based on capacity, Eq. 4, each stage’s setup cost $c_i^s$ divided by its capacity $u_i$.

The maximum inventory storage constraint can be modeled as an upper bound on $y$.

Example 5(a): Optimal plan

Determine the plan and its cost with Model 3.

```julia
# Code block 20: Ex. 5's data
u = [40, 80]                    # capacity of each stage (ton)
d = [25, 15, 10, 50, 25, 15]    # demand in each period (ton)
# variable production cost for each stage ($/ton)
cᵖ = [200, 800]
cˢ = [6000, 18000]              # setup cost for each stage ($/month)
h = 0.4/12                    # monthly inventory carrying rate (1/month)
# inventory cost for each stage ($/ton)
@show cⁱ = cumsum(cᵖ + cˢ./u)*h
y⁰ = [5, 25]                    # initial inventory of each stage (ton)
yᵗ⁺¹ = [10, 15]                 # final inventory of each stage (ton)

t = length(d)                   # number of periods of production
# same LB and UB to fix initial and final inventory levels
LBʸ = [y⁰ zeros(m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹]
UBʸ = [y⁰ fill(30, m, t-1) yᵗ⁺¹];  # max inventory storage level
```
