Example 5(b): Cost of a given plan by hand

Using some different data as noted below (otherwise, use the data given in Ex. 5) and only a three-month planning horizon, determine the total variable production, inventory, and setup cost over the horizon. The forecasted demand is 22, 3, and 33 tons per month. The product loses five percent of its value after one month. Each month, 20, 4, 40 and 25, 0, 37 tons, respectively, are produced at each stage. Currently, five tons of material is in storage at stage one and none at stage two; at the end of the planning period, seven tons of material should be in storage at stage one and four at stage two.

The production values, the inputs to the network, are given, so the missing data can be inferred using the flow balance equations, as in Exs. 2 and 3, and the costs then computed from them.

Going month by month, the inventory carried out of each node is what came in less what went on:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y_{1,2} &= 5 + 20 - 25 = 0, &\qquad y_{2,2} &= 0 + 25 - 22 = 3, \\
y_{1,3} &= 0 + 4 - 0 = 4, & y_{2,3} &= 3 + 0 - 3 = 0, \\
y_{1,4} &= 4 + 40 - 37 = 7, & y_{2,4} &= 0 + 37 - 33 = 4
\end{aligned}

$$

The final inventories come out at the 7 and 4 tons required, the Balance check of Lecture 1.2. The product losing five percent of its value in a month is a carrying rate of $h = 0.05$ per month, and with the setup share of assumption (e) the inventory costs are $c_1^i = 0.05\,(200 + 6{,}000/40) = 17.50$ and $c_2^i = 0.05\,(200 + 6{,}000/40 + 800 + 18{,}000/80) = 68.75$ \$/ton-month. Stage 1 produces in all three months and stage 2 in months 1 and 3, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{production:}\quad & 200\,(20 + 4 + 40) + 800\,(25 + 0 + 37) = 62{,}400 \\
\text{inventory:}\quad & 17.50\,(0 + 4 + 7) + 68.75\,(3 + 0 + 4) = 673.75 \\
\text{setups:}\quad & 6{,}000\,(3) + 18{,}000\,(2) = 54{,}000
\end{aligned}

$$

Code block 27 computes the same three costs from the plan, and checks them against the answers published with the problem, the Landmark check of Lecture 1.2:

```julia
# Code block 27: Ex. 5(b)'s plan, costed
X = [20 4 40; 25 0 37]              # production at stage i in month j
db = [22, 3, 33]                    # demand in month j
Y = zeros(2, 4)                     # inventory, by flow balance
Y[:, 1] = [5, 0]
for j in 1:3
    Y[1, j+1] = Y[1, j] + X[1, j] - X[2, j]
    Y[2, j+1] = Y[2, j] + X[2, j] - db[j]
end
@assert Y[:, 4] == [7, 4]           # the final inventories required
cⁱb = cumsum(cᵖ + cˢ./u)*0.05       # monthly carrying rate 0.05
Z = X .> 0                          # a setup wherever there is production
VPC, IC, SC = sum(cᵖ.*X), sum(cⁱb.*Y[:, 2:end]), sum(cˢ.*Z)
@assert all((VPC, IC, SC) .≈ (62400, 673.75, 54000))  # published
@show VPC
@show IC
@show SC;
```

```text
VPC = 62400
IC = 673.75
SC = 54000
```

Variable production cost \$62,400, inventory cost \$673.75, and setup cost \$54,000, for a total of \$117,073.75.

What drives the decision to produce in a period is whether its setup cost is worth incurring, and what counts as a setup cost varies. In baking, firing up the oven costs about the same for one loaf of bread as for a hundred, so that cost can be treated as a setup cost, while the variable cost is mostly the ingredients: the more bread, the more flour. Whether to fire up the oven on a given day or sell bread from the day before is the same trade-off as in Ex. 5, although bread goes stale, so the oven is probably fired up every day; other resources would go unused in some periods. Transportation is the same phenomenon, set up differently. Thought of in more general terms, transportation is a kind of production, the production of a movement, and a truckload is at the other extreme from the oven. Moving a tractor-trailer from one point to another costs very nearly the same with one box in it as completely full, since most of the cost is the truck itself and its driver, who is paid either way; only the fuel varies slightly, mostly with wind resistance. Easily 90 or 95 percent of the cost is independent of the quantity in the truck,3 so as a good approximation it is all setup cost.

The Transport lectures give a transport stage its costs. The truckload charge can be viewed as the setup cost, with effectively almost no variable cost, since the charge is essentially for the truck and trailer. Ex. 6 is the transport counterpart of Ex. 5’s manufacturing.

Example 6: Truckload as a setup cost

The product of Ex. 1 in Lecture 3.3, 20 tons a year of 40-lb, 9-ft³ cartons valued at \$25,000 a ton and carried at 0.3 \$/\$-yr, is shipped by truckload 532 miles from Raleigh (27606) to Gainesville (32606) at January 2018 rates. Plan its shipments week by week over a year as Model 3, with a demand of 20/52 tons a week at Gainesville and no inventory at either end of the year: (a) determine the plan; and (b) determine it again at a value of \$85,000 a ton.

The plan has two stages. Stage 1 is the plant, which can produce any amount in a week at the product’s value, \$25,000 a ton, with no setup cost. Stage 2 is the shipment by truckload, set up once for each truck sent, at one truck’s charge, with no cost per ton and a capacity per setup of the maximum payload; any number of trucks can be sent in a week. The inventory at Gainesville carries the product’s value plus the truckload charge per ton, assumption (e) of Model 3, which is Lecture 3.3’s allocated full-truckload rate, Ex. 1(h).

The cost of having a truck is found from the truck rate, and that cost becomes the setup cost of the production-inventory problem: every time a truck comes, its cost is incurred, the same kind of cost as a setup.

Code block 28 repeats the data of Lecture 3.3, Ex. 1, and the charge for one truck:

```julia

Kwt, Kcu = 25, 2750                 # trailer limits (ton, ft^3)
@show qmax = maxpayld(s; Kwt = Kwt, Kcu = Kcu)   # ton
f = 20                              # ton/yr
d = 532                             # mi, Raleigh to Gainesville
ppiTL, ppiLTL = 131.0, 177.4        # PPIs for Jan 2018
rTL = 2.00ppiTL/102.7               # $/mi
cTL = charge_tl(qmax, s, d; r = rTL, Kwt = Kwt, Kcu = Kcu,
                ppi = ppiTL)        # $/truck
@show cTL;
```

Example 6(a): Weekly plan

Determine the weekly plan for the year.

Code block 29 builds the year’s data for Model 3 from the truck’s charge and payload, as a function of the product’s value v, so that part (b) can change it, and solves it:

```julia
# Code block 29: the year planned week by week, at product value v
using Statistics
function weekly(v)
    weeks, h = 52, 0.3              # weeks in the year; carrying rate
    dw = fill(f/weeks, weeks)       # demand at Gainesville (ton/week)
    cᵖ = [v, 0.0]                   # plant; truck ($/ton)
    cˢ = [0.0, cTL]                 # setup costs ($/setup)
    u = [f, qmax]                   # capacity per setup (ton)
    z̄ = [ones(Int, 1, weeks);       # most setups in a week: the plant,
         fill(10, 1, weeks)]        #   and trucks, more than ever needed
    cⁱ = h/weeks .* [v, v + cTL/qmax]   # inventory cost ($/ton-week)
    LBʸ = zeros(2, weeks + 1)           # no inventory at either end
    UBʸ = [zeros(2) fill(Inf, 2, weeks - 1) zeros(2)]
    return prodinv_setup(cᵖ, cˢ, cⁱ, dw, u, z̄, LBʸ, UBʸ)
end
r25 = weekly(25000)
tl25 = findall(>(0), r25.z[2, :])              # weeks a truck is sent
@show length(tl25)
@show mean(r25.x[2, tl25])                     # tons per truck
mean(diff(tl25))                               # weeks between trucks
```

## 4. Forecasting demand

Every model so far has taken the demand in each period, $d_j$, as given. In practice, the initial periods of a planning horizon are probably occupied primarily by orders already booked: the orders already received are used to populate demand. Toward the end of the horizon the orders thin out, and rather than demand decreasing over the horizon, new orders will be received. That is where traditional forecasting is applied, based on some type of recent history, to forecast the likely orders, especially for products that have seasonality or are not expected to be constant.

The demand over the planning horizon typically comes from a corporate information technology environment, a master production schedule or a material requirements planning (MRP) or enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, which holds the best information available. That information is a mix: for some periods the demand is just a forecast, and for others there are firm orders, customers promised delivery six months out, say. In some businesses the demand going forward is the aggregate of the orders actually received, and little forecasting is done at all: everything to be produced over the next year is produced against firm orders in hand. In a company, the demand comes down a planning hierarchy. Sales and operations planning sets a plan for each family of products, typically monthly and a year or more out; master scheduling turns it into a master production schedule (MPS) for each product, which says what will be made in each period of the planning horizon; and MRP uses the bills of material to work out every component the MPS needs and when to order it. Going down the hierarchy, the detail increases and the horizon shrinks.4 An enterprise resource planning (ERP) system is a software system that controls the entire operations of a firm. The item, carrier, and customer master files are maintained by an ERP system and are used as a common data source for orders.

Of the three scope levels of logistics decisions in Lecture 1.1, Sec. 2, strategic (years), tactical (weeks to a year) and operational (minutes to a week), the production-inventory models of Secs. 2 and 3 are tactical. The demand is a mix of firm and forecasted orders: further out, more of it is forecast, and the more immediate periods have more actual booked orders. Planning guides draw the same shape as a curve, the cumulative orders on hand displacing the forecast the closer a period comes to the present.5 An order that has been booked was part of the forecast, so it cannot simply be added to it. Planning systems let orders consume the forecast: within a short window starting at the present, the demand time fence, only the orders booked count; beyond it, one of several common rules uses the larger of the forecast and the orders already booked.6 Fig. 5 draws both: the orders on hand displacing the forecast as a period comes closer, and the rule on either side of the fence.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 32: orders on hand consuming the forecast
let
    F = [0.85, 1.10, 0.80, 0.95, 1.00, 0.70, 0.95, 1.20, 1.05, 0.80]
    n, fence = length(F), 2            # periods ahead, demand time fence
    ordc, fcc = colorant"#1f5fa8", colorant"#b9cde5"
    grey = colorant"#bdbdbd"
    s = [max(0.0, 1 - (ℓ - 1)/6)^1.4 for ℓ in 1:n]  # share usually booked
    b = s .* F                         # orders on hand
    b[4] = 1.18                        # booked beyond its forecast
    fig = Figure(size = (680, 350))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Periods ahead", ylabel = "Demand",
              xticks = 1:n)
    hideydecorations!(ax; label = false)
    for ℓ in 1:n
        poly!(ax, Rect2f(ℓ - 0.4, 0, 0.8, b[ℓ]); color = ordc)
        if b[ℓ] < F[ℓ] && ℓ <= fence   # forecast set aside
            poly!(ax, Rect2f(ℓ - 0.4, b[ℓ], 0.8, F[ℓ] - b[ℓ]);
                  color = :white, strokecolor = grey, strokewidth = 1)
        elseif b[ℓ] < F[ℓ]             # forecast not yet booked
            poly!(ax, Rect2f(ℓ - 0.4, b[ℓ], 0.8, F[ℓ] - b[ℓ]);
                  color = fcc)
        elseif b[ℓ] > F[ℓ]             # the forecast, below the orders
            lines!(ax, [ℓ - 0.4, ℓ + 0.4], [F[ℓ], F[ℓ]]; color = :white,
                   linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.6)
        end
    end
    text!(ax, 4, F[4] + 0.03; text = "forecast", fontsize = 11,
          color = :white, align = (:center, :bottom))
    text!(ax, 4, b[4] + 0.04; fontsize = 11, align = (:center, :bottom),
          text = "orders exceed\nthe forecast:\nplan on the orders")
    vlines!(ax, [fence + 0.5]; color = ink, linestyle = :dash,
            linewidth = 1.2)
    text!(ax, fence + 0.6, 1.85; text = "demand time fence",
          fontsize = 12, align = (:left, :bottom))
    text!(ax, (fence + 1)/2, 1.38; text = "orders only", fontsize = 12,
          align = (:center, :bottom))
    text!(ax, 7.6, 1.38; text = "the larger of\nforecast and orders",
          fontsize = 12, align = (:center, :bottom))
    arrows2d!(ax, [9.6], [0.42], [-5.8], [0]; color = ink,
              shaftwidth = 1.2, tipwidth = 8, tiplength = 8)
    text!(ax, 7.0, 0.46; fontsize = 11, align = (:center, :bottom),
          text = "as a period comes closer, orders replace its forecast")
    elem = [PolyElement(color = ordc), PolyElement(color = fcc),
            PolyElement(color = :white, strokecolor = grey,
                        strokewidth = 1)]
    Legend(fig[2, 1], elem,
           ["Orders on hand", "Forecast", "Forecast set aside"];
           orientation = :horizontal, framevisible = false,
           labelsize = 12)
    xlims!(ax, 0.4, n + 0.6); ylims!(ax, 0, 2.05); hidespines!(ax, :t, :r)
    fig
end
```

Figure 5: Schematic of the orders on hand consuming the forecast, for a demand that varies from period to period. The nearer a period, the more of its demand is already booked (dark blue) and the less is forecast (light blue). Within the demand time fence only the orders count, and the forecast not yet booked is set aside; beyond it the plan uses the larger of the forecast and the orders, so in period 4, where the orders already exceed the forecast (dashed), it plans on the orders.

The more immediate periods typically have better forecasts, and the further into the future, the less accurate the forecasts become. A forecast is always wrong, so it should come with a measure of its error, measured at the lead at which the forecast is acted on, since the error grows with the lead; and simple methods are hard to beat.7 8 How long a horizon should be, the subject of Sec. 5, depends on that growth of the error with the lead.

## 5. Planning horizon

How is the planning horizon determined? It has to be long enough to incorporate any decision that affects the production of the product over time. If something plays itself out in two or three weeks, a horizon of a month is more than adequate, whereas a production process that has to be shut down for month-long maintenance may need a horizon of two or three years, to incorporate several of its maintenance downtimes into the plan.

Not every product needs a long horizon. One that takes three or four days to make, from materials in hand or easy to get, on resources available most of the month, needs no plan of several months: a week ahead is enough, and that is production scheduling, not a problem for these models. The models are for decisions that take months to play out. One is maintenance: resources that each have to be down for two months every three years need to be taken down at the best times, never in the peak season and staggered so that together they disrupt the least, given the best estimate of demand. Another is lead time: with a material that takes four or five months to arrive once ordered, production waits until the material is in hand rather than holding work in process for months.

Oil refineries, for example, plan month by month but typically about 36 months ahead, a window within which each refinery is taken down for one, two or three months of scheduled maintenance.9 Given an estimate of demand, the models work out when to take each resource down so that several are not down at once, which makes them a planning tool for a complex organization.

The length of the horizon should include all significant planning decisions, and one of the main ones is scheduled maintenance. In one study of power plants in Saudi Arabia, maintenance was done in the winter, when demand was lower than in the summer, and the plan looked about three years ahead to determine which plants would be down for maintenance, and when, while still meeting demand.

A typical number of periods is anywhere from six to 36; with monthly periods, three years of monthly data is common. With weekly periods, a plan might look 26 weeks ahead.

The research literature calls a horizon long enough that nothing beyond it can change the first period’s decision a forecast horizon.10 11 Four questions follow, in turn: how a plan uses its horizon, how long the horizon must be, why it should not be longer, and how a choice of horizon is checked. Fig. 6 draws the first two for a resource with an outage ahead, its materials ordered two periods before the period that uses them.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 33: rolling plans ahead of an outage, with a lead time
let
    T, δ = 12, 2                       # periods, lead time
    cap, o = 0.7, 9:10                 # capacity, periods of the outage
    d = [0.50, 0.33, 0.46, 0.37, 0.47, 0.41,
         0.42, 0.41, 0.41, 0.42, 0.43, 0.44]  # demand
    planc, ordc = colorant"#b9cde5", colorant"#1f5fa8"
    idlec, invc = colorant"#9ccf9c", colorant"#e08a1e"
    grey = colorant"#bdbdbd"
    nb, sp = 0, 0.0                    # count back from the outage
    while sp < sum(d[o])
        nb += 1
        sp += cap - d[o[1] - nb]
    end
    b0 = o[1] - nb                     # first period of the build-ahead
    a0 = b0 - δ                        # its materials are ordered
    H = δ + nb + length(o)
    rows = T - H + 1                   # plans whose window fits
    fig = Figure(size = (680, 640))
    # (a) a plan made in each period: its first δ periods already
    # ordered, the period δ ahead ordered now, the rest planned
    ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xticks = 1:T, ylabel = "Plan made in period",
               yticks = 1:rows, yreversed = true, titlesize = 13,
               titlefont = :regular,
               title = rich("(a) Rolling: plan ",
                   it("H"), up(" = $H"), " periods ahead; ",
                   "order for the period a lead time away"))
    hidespines!(ax1, :t, :r)
    vspan!(ax1, [b0 - 0.5], [o[1] - 0.5]; color = (idlec, 0.35))
    vspan!(ax1, [o[1] - 0.5], [o[end] + 0.5]; color = (datac, 0.18))
    for k in 1:rows
        J = k:min(k + H - 1, T)
        for j in J
            if j < k + δ               # already ordered
                poly!(ax1, Rect2f(j - 0.43, k - 0.30, 0.86, 0.60);
                      color = :white, strokecolor = ordc,
                      strokewidth = 1.2)
            else
                poly!(ax1, Rect2f(j - 0.45, k - 0.32, 0.9, 0.64);
                      color = j == k + δ ? ordc : planc,
                      strokecolor = :white)
            end
        end
        # inventory carried in at the window's start, out at its end
        scatter!(ax1, [k - 0.5], [k]; marker = :rtriangle,
                 markersize = 9, color = invc)
        last(J) == k + H - 1 &&
            scatter!(ax1, [last(J) + 0.5], [k]; marker = :rtriangle,
                     markersize = 9, color = invc)
    end
    poly!(ax1, Rect2f(a0 - 0.5, a0 - 0.42, H, 0.84);
          color = :transparent, strokecolor = ink, strokewidth = 1.4)
    text!(ax1, 0.6, a0 + 1.6; fontsize = 11, align = (:left, :center),
          text = "the outlined plan, made\nin period $a0, " *
                 "orders for\nperiod $b0, the first of the\n" *
                 "build-ahead, so it has\nto see past the outage")
    xlims!(ax1, 0.4, T + 0.6); ylims!(ax1, rows + 0.6, 0.4)
    elem = [PolyElement(color = :white, strokecolor = ordc,
                        strokewidth = 1.2),
            PolyElement(color = ordc), PolyElement(color = planc),
            MarkerElement(marker = :rtriangle, color = invc,
                          markersize = 9)]
    Legend(fig[2, 1], elem,
           ["Already ordered", "Ordered now", "Planned, not yet ordered",
            "Inventory carried in at the start and out at the end"];
           orientation = :horizontal, nbanks = 2, framevisible = false,
           labelsize = 12)
    # (b) the horizon of the outlined plan: from its order to the end
    # of the outage, each period's materials ordered δ periods ahead
    ax2 = Axis(fig[3, 1]; xlabel = "Period", xticks = 1:T,
               titlesize = 13, titlefont = :regular,
               title = "(b) How long: from the first build-ahead " *
                       "order to the end of the outage")
    hideydecorations!(ax2); hidespines!(ax2, :t, :r, :l)
    for j in 1:T
        if b0 <= j < o[1]              # idle capacity builds inventory
            poly!(ax2, Rect2f(j - 0.45, d[j], 0.9, cap - d[j]);
                  color = idlec)
        end
        poly!(ax2, Rect2f(j - 0.45, 0, 0.9, d[j]);
              color = j in o ? datac : grey)
    end
    lines!(ax2, [0.5, o[1] - 0.5, o[1] - 0.5, o[end] + 0.5,
                 o[end] + 0.5, T + 0.5], [cap, cap, 0, 0, cap, cap];
           color = ink, linewidth = 1.5)
    for k in a0:(o[1] - 1 - δ)         # one order a period, δ ahead
        xs = range(k, k + δ; length = 40)
        lines!(ax2, xs, cap + 0.04 .+ 0.13 .* sin.(π .* (xs .- k) ./ δ);
               color = ordc, linewidth = 1.4)
        scatter!(ax2, [k], [cap + 0.04]; markersize = 5, color = ordc)
        scatter!(ax2, [k + δ], [cap + 0.04]; marker = :dtriangle,
                 markersize = 8, color = ordc)
    end
    text!(ax2, a0 + δ/2, cap + 0.19; text = it("δ"),
          fontsize = 13, color = ordc, align = (:center, :bottom))
    text!(ax2, a0 - 0.6, cap + 0.21; fontsize = 11, color = ordc,
          align = (:right, :center),
          text = "one order each\nperiod, a lead\ntime ahead")
    text!(ax2, T + 0.4, cap + 0.02; text = "capacity", fontsize = 12,
          align = (:right, :bottom))
    text!(ax2, 0.6, 0.05; text = "demand", fontsize = 12,
          align = (:left, :bottom))
    text!(ax2, (b0 + o[1] - 1)/2, cap - 0.03; fontsize = 11,
          align = (:center, :top),
          text = "idle capacity\nbuilds inventory")
    text!(ax2, (o[1] + o[end])/2, d[o[end]] + 0.03; text = "outage",
          fontsize = 12, color = datac, align = (:center, :bottom))
    bracket!(ax2, a0 - 0.45, cap + 0.33, o[end] + 0.45, cap + 0.33;
             text = rich(it("H"), up(" ≥ "), it("δ"), up(" + "),
                         "build-ahead", up(" + "), "outage"),
             fontsize = 12, style = :square, color = ink,
             textcolor = ink, textoffset = 18)
    xlims!(ax2, 0.4, T + 0.6); ylims!(ax2, 0, 1.4)
    linkxaxes!(ax1, ax2)
    rowsize!(fig.layout, 1, Relative(0.5))
    fig
end
```

Figure 6: Schematic of rolling plans ahead of an outage, with materials ordered two periods before the period that uses them. (a) A plan is made in each period over a horizon of $H = 7$ periods: its first two periods were ordered by the plans before it (outlined), it orders the materials for the period two ahead (dark blue), and the rest is planned but not yet ordered (light blue); each plan starts from the inventory carried in and ends with the inventory carried out (orange). (b) The idle capacity of periods 6 to 8 (green) builds the inventory that covers the demand of the outage in periods 9 and 10 (red). Each period orders for the period two ahead, so the plan made in period 4, outlined in (a), is the earliest that has to see to the end of the outage, and $H \ge \delta$ + build-ahead + outage.

How a plan uses its horizon. A plan is acted on only in its first period. For Ex. 1’s plan, the manager is told to produce 45 tons at each stage in period 1. The later periods are not acted on, but they are part of the planning: how much to produce now depends on how much will be carried over as inventory and how much produced later. A month later the model is run again, and the second period becomes the first. Even if no demand has changed, a planned maintenance may have moved and freed capacity, which changes the plan from the inventory carried over; and each new run adds an estimate of the demand one more period out, which can change what is done now. Problems of realistic size give almost no insight just by looking at them.

The work flow of a planning model in use, as Fig. 7 draws it, runs in five steps:

$$
\text{Data} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Model} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Solver} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Output} \;\rightarrow\; \text{Report}

$$

Reports are run on a regular period-to-period, rolling-horizon basis as part of normal operations management. The model is only changed when the logistics network changes.

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia
# Code block 34: the logistics software stack
let
    boxc, edgec = colorant"#dff2da", colorant"#3a8a4f"
    # name, what it is, centre (x, y); every box 6.65 wide and 2.5 high
    B = [("Data", "csv, Excel, etc.", (4.0, -1.3)),
         ("Report", "GUI, web, etc.", (11.3, -1.3)),
         ("Scripting", "Python, Matlab, Julia", (7.62, -5.92)),
         ("User Library", "in script language", (16.15, -5.92)),
         ("MIP Solver", "Gurobi, Cplex, etc.", (4.0, -10.55)),
         ("Standard Library", "in compiled C, Java", (11.3, -10.55))]
    w, h, rr = 6.65, 2.5, 0.9                     # width, height, corner
    function rbox(c)                              # a rounded box outline
        x0, y0 = c[1] - w/2 + rr, c[2] - h/2 + rr
        x1, y1 = c[1] + w/2 - rr, c[2] + h/2 - rr
        arc(xc, yc, a) = [Point2f(xc + rr*cos(θ), yc + rr*sin(θ))
                          for θ in range(a, a + π/2; length = 12)]
        cs = [(x1, y0, -π/2), (x1, y1, 0), (x0, y1, π/2), (x0, y0, π)]
        return reduce(vcat, [arc(k...) for k in cs])  # corner by corner
    end
    fig = Figure(size = (680, 430))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; aspect = DataAspect())
    hidedecorations!(ax); hidespines!(ax)
    # what commercial software packages, dashed
    lines!(ax, [0.05, 19.95, 19.95, 0.05, 0.05],
           [-3.65, -3.65, -12.35, -12.35, -3.65];
           color = ink, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5)
    text!(ax, 17.45, -9.55;
          text = "Commercial\nSoftware\n(LLamasoft, etc.)",
          align = (:center, :center), justification = :center,
          fontsize = 15, color = ink)
    # each arrow from box edge to box edge; the last three run both ways
    for (p, q, both) in [((4.0, -2.55), (6.15, -4.67), false),   # data in
                         ((9.25, -4.67), (11.25, -2.55), false), # report
                         ((10.945, -5.92), (12.825, -5.92), true),
                         ((6.1, -7.17), (4.1, -9.3), true),
                         ((9.3, -7.17), (11.25, -9.3), true)]
        for (a, b) in (both ? [(p, q), (q, p)] : [(p, q)])
            arrows2d!(ax, [a[1]], [a[2]], [b[1] - a[1]], [b[2] - a[2]];
                      color = datac, shaftwidth = 2.2, tipwidth = 11,
                      tiplength = 11)
        end
    end
    for (name, what, c) in B                      # boxes, over the arrows
        poly!(ax, rbox(c); color = boxc, strokecolor = edgec,
              strokewidth = 2)
        text!(ax, c[1], c[2] + 0.45; text = name, fontsize = 17,
              font = :bold, color = ink, align = (:center, :center))
        text!(ax, c[1], c[2] - 0.55; text = "($what)", fontsize = 14,
              color = ink, align = (:center, :center))
    end
    xlims!(ax, -0.2, 20.2); ylims!(ax, -12.6, 0.0)
    fig
end
```

Figure 7: The logistics software stack, the work flow of a planning model in use: the data go into a script, which calls a MIP solver and its libraries and turns the output into a report. Commercial software, such as LLamasoft’s, packages everything inside the dashed line.

With the models of this lecture done, the overall work flow can be seen better. The first step is getting the data, and for a model run every week or every month, getting them is worth automating: fed in from whatever system the company uses, its forecast of demand, say, and whatever other information is needed, so that they are taken into the model on a regular basis without much work. A scripting language, Julia, Matlab or Python, is a good way of getting the data: it takes them in whatever form they come, from a database or elsewhere, and converts them into what the mathematical programming model needs.

The script then calls the solver, and the last piece is reporting the results in a user-friendly way. With 20 plants, not every plant manager needs the entire output of the run: each is sent what that plant should produce over the next several periods, the output focused on each entity in the logistics network. Data, model, solver, output and report is the basic flow.

How long the horizon must be. A plan’s final inventory stands in for every period beyond its horizon, and with nothing required at its end, a plan too short to see a coming outage will not build for it. The cumulative lead time $\delta$ is the longest chain of purchasing and production lead times.

Each period’s materials are ordered $\delta$ periods ahead of the period that uses them, so the first $\delta$ periods of every plan are already committed by orders placed in the periods before, and the decision a plan made now acts on is the order for period $\delta + 1$; with the materials on hand, $\delta = 0$.12 A plan therefore looks at least $\delta$ periods ahead, and further when the order placed now depends on what comes after the period it supplies. For an outage, a count estimates how much further. Scheduled maintenance is one of the important reasons to plan several periods ahead: the plan has to make sure that enough inventory is on hand to cover the maintenance.

An outage with no other source. This count is the machine-hours accounting of Lecture 1.3, Sec. 5, done one period at a time. A resource at utilization $u$ (Eq. 5 in Lecture 1.3) has idle capacity of $1 - u$ of what it can produce in a period. Lecture 1.3 warned that $u < 1$ holds only on average, and a scheduled outage is a burst of demand over capacity that is known in advance and too long to average away. The plan builds the inventory for it on the idle capacity of the periods before it: counting back from the outage, each period’s idle capacity is added until the total covers the outage’s demand, and the horizon has to span those periods and the outage. The plan that has to see the outage is the one that orders the materials for the first period of the build-ahead, $\delta$ periods before it, the plan outlined in Fig. 6; each later period’s materials are ordered by a later plan, which sees the outage as well. At a steady utilization $u$ the count can be done in closed form. Measure demand and inventory in periods of the resource’s production, so that each period’s demand is $u$ and its idle capacity $1 - u$. An outage of $\tau$ periods then has a demand of $\tau u$, all of it to be built ahead, and $b$ periods of build-ahead supply $b\,(1 - u)$ of it, so the number of periods of build-ahead satisfies:

$$
b\,(1 - u) = \tau u, \qquad b = \frac{\tau u}{1 - u}

$$

The plan that has to see the outage spans, in turn, the $\delta$ periods already committed at its front, the $b$ periods of build-ahead and the $\tau$ periods of the outage, the three spans Fig. 6(b) brackets, so its horizon is at least their sum. With $b$ substituted, and since $\tau u + \tau (1 - u) = \tau$, the sum is Eq. 5:

$$
H \ge \delta + b + \tau = \delta + \frac{\tau u}{1 - u} + \tau = \delta + \frac{\tau}{1 - u}
\tag{5}
$$

where

- $H$ = planning horizon (periods)
- $\delta$ = cumulative lead time (periods)
- $\tau$ = length of the outage (periods)
- $u$ = utilization of the resource in the periods before the outage.

By Eq. 5, with materials on hand ($\delta = 0$), a month-long outage at 90% utilization needs a horizon of 10 months, and at 95%, 20; a lead time adds to each. The horizon grows as $1/(1-u)$, the factor by which cycle time grows in Lecture 1.3’s VUT equation (Eq. 6 in Lecture 1.3): a busy resource has little idle capacity to build ahead with, which is one reason a month of maintenance can call for years of planning; the other is that the plan has to span the maintenance cycle, so that it can determine when each plant is down.

The lead time is counted once in Eq. 5, not once for each period of the build-ahead, because the materials for a build-ahead are not all ordered at one time and left to sit for two or three periods; they are ordered each period, so a two-period lead time overlaps each period of the build-ahead.

Why it should not be longer. The plan is re-solved every period, so the numbers get less certain the further out they are, and are more subject to change.

Each run can also change what was planned for the coming periods, which unsettles everyone who works to the plan; companies damp this by freezing the nearest periods of the plan, at some cost.13

A longer horizon can also break the model: one that solves well can go to running for 80 hours without stopping when one more variable is added, or when the horizon goes from 12 periods to 18. These models assume the demand will be satisfied exactly as planned; safety stock applies only to the current period.

How a horizon is checked. Solve with $H$ and again with a longer one: if neither the first period’s decision nor the cost of the plan acted on changes, $H$ was long enough for these data, the Nudge check of Lecture 1.2. As Sec. 1 said, more than one horizon can be defended; what makes the choice right is its reason.

Example 7: Horizon of the month-1 plan

Ex. 1’s product, with Ex. 1’s costs, has a forecast of demand and a schedule of capacities for the next six months, the three of Ex. 1 and three more, starting and ending with no inventory. The capacities of its two stages and the demand in the six months are, in tons,

$$
\begin{gathered}
u = \begin{bmatrix} 50 & 0 & 50 & 0 & 0 & 50 \\ 60 & 0 & 0 & 60 & 60 & 60 \end{bmatrix}, \\[4pt]
d = \begin{bmatrix} 20 & 10 & 15 & 20 & 15 & 25 \end{bmatrix}.
\end{gathered}

$$

The six months are the data available, not the horizon. Determine by hand how many of them a plan made in month 1 has to look ahead, and the plan over all six months.

This is a two-stage, six-month example. It is the same as Ex. 1, except that the figure of Ex. 1’s network showed only the first three periods; otherwise the data are the same.

Starting and ending with no inventory, as this example and Ex. 6 do, is rare in practice, since these are typically ongoing operations; the zeros are a simplification.

Example 7(a): By hand

Determine the horizon from the capacities and the demand, before any plan is solved.

Stage 2 has no capacity in months 2 and 3, an outage of two months, so their demand, 10 and 15 tons, has to be made in month 1. In the terms of Eq. 5’s count, with the materials on hand ($\delta = 0$), stage 2’s idle capacity in month 1, 60 − 20 = 40 tons, covers the outage’s 25 tons, so the build-ahead is one month, and the plan made in month 1 has to span it and the outage: $H \ge 0 + 1 + 2 = 3$ months. That is an estimate committed before any plan is solved, the Prior check of Lecture 1.2.

Example 7(b): In Julia

Determine the plan over all six months.

Code block 35 enters the six months, Ex. 1’s three and the next three, and solves them with Model 1:

```julia
# Code block 35: the six-month plan
u6 = [50  0 50  0  0 50;          # capacity of stage i in period j (ton)
      60  0  0 60 60 60]
d6 = [20, 10, 15, 20, 15, 25]       # demand in period j (ton)
cᵖ = [200, 800]                     # production cost in stage i ($/ton)
cⁱ = cumsum(cᵖ)*0.3/12              # inventory cost for stage i ($/ton)
LBʸ = zeros(2, 7)                   # no inventory at the start or end
UBʸ = [zeros(2) fill(Inf, 2, 5) zeros(2)]
TC6, x6, y6 = prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d6, u6, LBʸ, UBʸ)
@show TC6
prt(y6; rows = ["1", "2"], cols = string.(1:7),
    row_title = "Stage")              # inventory into each month
```

```text
TC6 = 106250.0
Stage  1   2   3   4   5  6  7
──────────────────────────────
    1  0   0   0  35  15  0  0
    2  0  25  15   0   0  0  0
```

The plan carries 35 tons of stage-1 inventory out of month 3, because stage 1 has no capacity in months 4 and 5 and stage 2 needs it to meet their demand. That is where Ex. 1’s final inventory of 35 tons at stage 1 came from: Ex. 1 is the first three months of this plan, and its final inventory stands in for the months beyond its horizon. The plan also agrees with the count of Ex. 7(a): stage 2 makes 45 tons in month 1, the demand of months 1 to 3, and carries 25 and 15 tons of it into months 2 and 3.

NoteCheck the horizon using Julia

Code block 36 checks the count of Ex. 7(a). It solves the plan made in month 1 with Model 1 over each horizon $H$ from one month to six, with nothing required at its end, and keeps each plan’s month-1 production, the decision that is acted on:

```julia
# Code block 36: the plan made in month 1, over horizons of 1 to 6 months
x₁ = zeros(2, 6)                    # month-1 production, horizon H
for H in 1:6
    LBʸ = zeros(2, H + 1)           # no inventory at the start or end
    UBʸ = [zeros(2) fill(Inf, 2, H - 1) zeros(2)]
    x₁[:, H] = prodinv(cᵖ, cⁱ, d6[1:H], u6[:, 1:H], LBʸ, UBʸ).x[:, 1]
end
prt(x₁; rows = ["1", "2"], cols = ["H = $H" for H in 1:6],
    row_title = "Stage")              # month 1's production, by H
```

```text
Stage  H = 1  H = 2  H = 3  H = 4  H = 5  H = 6
───────────────────────────────────────────────
    1     20     30     45     45     45     45
    2     20     30     45     45     45     45
```

The month-1 decision changes until $H = 3$ and not after. With one month, stage 2 makes only month 1’s 20 tons, and with two, 30, so the plan made in month 2, with no capacity at stage 2 in months 2 and 3, cannot satisfy their demand; from three months on, every plan makes 45 tons at stage 2 in month 1, whatever it sees beyond. So 3 months is long enough for these data, as the count found, and a longer horizon leaves the first month’s decision unchanged: the check of a horizon stated above, the Nudge check of Lecture 1.2.

A plan made in month 1 has to look 3 months ahead; the plan over all six months costs \$106,250.
